title: python_info_condaenv_find() breaks on conda-meta/history file paths that contain spaces
description:
I am trying to interface R with a [proprietary conda environment](https://pro.arcgis.com/en/pro-app/latest/arcpy/get-started/what-is-arcpy-.htm) maintained by [Esri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esri). This environment includes the ArcPy site package which contains a bunch of geospatial operations that I am unfortunately dependent on for work.

I have created a cloned conda environment of this site package, but I'm getting the following error whenever I try to interface with `reticulate`.

```r
library(reticulate)
use_condaenv(condaenv = "C:/Program Files/ArcGIS/Pro/bin/Python/envs/arcgispro-py3-clone", required = T)
```

```
Error in normalizePath(path.expand(path), winslash, mustWork) : 
  path[1]="C:/conda.exe": The system cannot find the file specified
```

I understand that this is not a complete reproducible example due to the dependency on this proprietary software, but I'm hoping that it will still be possible to troubleshoot to some degree. 

### Edit:

This bug appears to be specific to `reticulate_1.24`. Specifically, [this commit](https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/commit/4f4699f7b845e5689e7a5c163fb31d4e43002126#diff-d471e62749e21aceb08e8b748ed9f063a15a0346049031390a025267aaee7a00) is breaking things for me. After downgrading to `reticulate_1.22` I am able to configure my ArcGIS Pro conda environment using the following parameters:

```r
# Specifying full path to conda env
reticulate::use_condaenv(condaenv = "C:/Program Files/ArcGIS/Pro/bin/Python/envs/arcgispro-py3-clone", required = T)

# Specifying condaenv name, and path to conda.bat
reticulate::use_condaenv(condaenv = "arcgispro-py3-clone", conda = "C:/Program Files/ArcGIS/Pro/bin/Python/envs/arcgispro-py3-clone/Scripts/conda.bat", required = T)
```

title: .globals$py_config is not updated when changing conda environment
description:
Hi @kevinushey and @t-kalinowski,  

I am working on an r-package and I want to use a specific miniconda python environment in the r package.
I notice however that after I use  ```reticulate::use_miniconda(condaenv = "r-eikon", required = T)``` the internal global package value ```.globals$required_python_version``` is updated to the r-eikon conda environment but the value of ```.globals$py_config``` is left at the old conda environment (r-reticulate).

This leads to very weird behavior. E.g. when calling ```reticulate::py_module_available``` will return that already installed python modules are not available. However when opening miniconda and running ```conda activate r-eikon``` and ```conda list``` these are shown as installed in the r-eikon environment.

A possible solution for this would be to again initialize_python as currently it is only initialized once and when changing environments it is not initialized again.
https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/da515709ea629f5a9258bf35a1e4632a03e642a2/R/package.R#L29-L56 
 
So maybe in ```use_python()``` after the following line:
https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/1523ef58a13ba987267e5f976813525bedd17366/R/use_python.R#L112

When there is a difference between ```.globals$required_python_version``` and ```.globals$py_config```

to add something analogue to this: 
```.globals$py_config <- initialize_python(some variables)```


Reproducible bug:

title: Knitting an R markdown with python chunks fails silently when importing packages (w/ `reticulate`)
description:
Hi all, 

I am trying to knit an R markdown file with python chunks using `reticulate` but the knitting process did not complete (the red button disappears and the knitting log was stuck at the python chunk and no output was created). The code in the python chunk imports a couple of packages. 
```python
import arviz as az
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pymc3 as pm
import pandas as pd
import theano.tensor as tt
print(f"Running on PyMC3 v{pm.__version__}")
print(f"Running on ArviZ v{az.__version__}")
```
After fiddling with it, the issue seems to be that only certain python packages when imported prevent the document from being knitted normally. Specifically for my case, PyMC3 causes issues but importing pandas, arviz, numpy, etc. works fine. However, running the above code interactively works normally and it also works when run in an R script. 

I am unsure what this is all about but it might be a bug since the knitting fails silently without any errors.

title: how to set width and height of matplotlib images in python Rmd chunks?
description:
hi thanks very much for this package which is very useful for including python chunks in Rmd documents.
Is there a way to control the height and width of the images produced in the chunks? I would like to make Rmd beamer slides with images from matplotlib which have reduced height, but full slide width (so you can write a few lines of commentary above/below the figure). 
The fig.width and fig.height have no effect on the image size, and that is documented as R-specific: https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown-cookbook/figure-size.html says The size of plots made in R can be controlled by the chunk option fig.width and fig.height (in inches).
Is there another way to control matplotlib figure height and width?
The out.height='25%' chunk option works for proportionally reducing the image size (both height and width), but I would like to reduce the height but maintain full width. is that possible?
Thanks and here is a zip file with MRE as Rmd source code with rendered PDF.
[slides.zip](https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/files/7907758/slides.zip)

title: `length()` overwrites `py_last_error()`
matplotlib.pyplot.plot() causing 'memory not mapped' segfault
description:
### Issue

When using `plt.plot()` in a call to `reticulate::py_run_string()` I encounter a 'memory not mapped' segfault.

---

### Steps to reproduce

1. Create a `Dockerfile` with the contents:
   ```Dockerfile
   FROM rocker/r-ver:latest
   
   RUN apt update && apt install -y python3 python3-dev python3-venv
   
   RUN Rscript -e 'install.packages("reticulate")'
   
   COPY test.R /root/
   ```

 
2. Create a file `test.R` (in the same location) with the contents:
   ```R

title: conda, numpy, and Windows
description:
I don't know if it is something that concerns {reticulate} - but I figured I should say something.

Using Actions on a package-repo that uses reticulate, I finally tracked down the problem to numpy - but it was a problem I saw only on Windows.

Here's a snippet:

```
Error: Error in py_module_import(module, convert = convert) : ImportError: 

IMPORTANT: PLEASE READ THIS FOR ADVICE ON HOW TO SOLVE THIS ISSUE!

Importing the numpy C-extensions failed. This error can happen for
many reasons, often due to issues with your setup or how NumPy was
installed.

We have compiled some common reasons and troubleshooting tips at:

    https://numpy.org/devdocs/user/troubleshooting-importerror.html

Please note and check the following:

  * The Python version is: Python3.10 from "C:\R\bin\x64\Rscript.exe"
  * The NumPy version is: "1.22.0"

and make sure that they are the versions you expect.
Please carefully study the documentation linked above for further help.

Original error was: DLL load failed while importing _multiarray_umath: The specified module could not be found.


Detailed traceback:
  File "D:\a\_temp\Library\reticulate\python\rpytools\loader.py", line 39, in _import_hook
    module = _import(
  File "C:\Users\RUNNER~1\AppData\Local\R-MINI~1\envs\R-RETI~1\lib\site-packages\numpy\__init__.py", line 144
Calls: <Anonymous> -> py_module_import
```


I was able to fix the problem using a [SO post](https://stackoverflow.com/a/62531033/1523865) - I found that if I set the env variable:

```
CONDA_DLL_SEARCH_MODIFICATION_ENABLE=1
```

It would solve the problem.

To make things "reproducible", I created a toy repo: https://github.com/ijlyttle/reticulate.numpy

title: Show python exception message by default
description:
Consider a simple misconfigured keras model like this:
```R
model <- keras_model_sequential(input_shape = c(28 * 28)) %>%
  layer_dense(units = 512, activation = "relu") %>%
  layer_dense(units = 10, activation = "softmax")

model %>% compile(
  optimizer = "rmsprop",
  loss = "categorical_crossentropy",
  metrics = c("accuracy"))


model %>% fit(k_random_uniform(c(4, 28*29)), 
              k_random_uniform(c(4,10)))
```
In Rstudio, this is what's visible after evaluating this chunk:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/8462255/148588455-9429c9cd-3970-4bc1-83e4-111526f15176.png)

This is problematic because it gives a lot of output, but nothing useful to the user about what caused the error. Expanding the stacktrace helps a little, but the actual message is in a big unformatted and unevaluated jumble of a template string (which is sometimes also truncated, though not in this example) 

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/8462255/148588678-71257e3a-ea4e-45f3-8d41-6db1ec411ce8.png)

Printing the actual exception shows a different message, which I'm guessing was generated by the IDE overwriting the original python error:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/8462255/148588819-d589bb29-4289-4928-8434-7d0d2f4216ff.png)

Note the actionable information that should be shown prominently to the user is usually available 
by running `for(m in reticulate::py_last_error()) cat(m)`, which would show this as a standalone, prominent line: 
```
ValueError: Input 0 of layer "sequential" is incompatible with the layer: expected shape=(None, 784), found shape=(None, 812)
```

It might even make sense to show the full python stack track as well (e.g., from a different example of an error message):

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/8462255/148586373-db0181b4-0a07-435d-b0d2-7d9b6a00ae8b.png)

title: Warning when `find_conda()` returns multiple conda locations
description:
I'm now seeing a warning when there are multiple conda's installed on a system:
```R
Warning in if (!grepl("^conda", basename(conda))) stop("Supplied path is not a conda binary: ",  :
  the condition has length > 1 and only the first element will be used
Warning in if (file.exists(altpath)) return(normalizePath(altpath, winslash = "/",  :
  the condition has length > 1 and only the first element will be used
```
I think this is because `find_conda()` can now return a character vector of length > 1:
https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/4da33563157f0b0ef50d1f4d267839627d5425fc/R/conda.R#L731

There are two uses I found where `find_conda()` is assumed to return a length 1 vector or NULL, in `py_discover_config_fallbacks()` and `conda_binary()`, which are both called during python initialization.

Should `find_conda()` be returning the `conda_locations[1]` here?

title: Cannot silence 'conda_create'
description:
Dear reticulate maintainers,

Thanks for reticulate! As I am using reticulate a lot because it works so well, I suggest something here to make it -in my opinion- even better: being able to call `reticulate::conda_create` silently.

Every time I call `reticulate::conda_create` in the tests of my own packages, it adds noise to the tests, as `reticulate::conda_create` produces output:

```r
  # Produces output, how to suppress this?
  reticulate::conda_create(
    envname = tempfile()
  )
```

Whatever I tried, I cannot silence this output either:

```r
  envname <- tempfile()

  # Produces output, how to suppress this?
  reticulate::conda_create(
    envname = envname
  )

  # Fails

  # Using 'reticulate::py_capture_output'
  reticulate::py_capture_output(
    reticulate::conda_create(
      envname = envname
    )
  )
  # Using suppressMessages
  suppressMessages(
    reticulate::conda_create(
      envname = envname
    )
  )
  # Using sink
  envname <- tempfile()
  sinkfile <- tempfile()
  sink(sinkfile)
  reticulate::conda_create(
    envname = envname
  )
  sink(NULL)
```

I suggest to allow `conda_create` to be silent, e.g. using a `verbose` function argument, e.g. allowing the code below to work:

```r
  # Should produce no output
  reticulate::conda_create(
    envname = tempfile(),
    verbose = FALSE
  )
```

If there is another workaround I missed, I'd love to hear it! Else, I hope this will be implemented: my tests are 90% filled with these reticulate messages :-/

Thanks and cheers, Richel Bilderbeek

title: find_conda() miniforge location on M1 Mac
description:
It may be useful to add `/opt/homebrew/Caskroom/miniforge` and `/opt/homebrew/miniforge` to the default search paths of `reticulate::find_conda()`. These are currently the default install paths when [installing miniforge via homebrew](https://docs.brew.sh/Installation). [`reticulate::find_conda()`](https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/dd6d6e8139dcfc4ce19e6b7150406a6f4e1af747/R/conda.R#L447-L452) only searches combinations of:

```
  prefixes <- c("~/opt/", "~/", "/opt/", "/")
  names <- c("anaconda", "miniconda", "miniforge")
  versions <- c("", "2", "3", "4")
  combos <- expand.grid(versions, names, prefixes, KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  combos <- combos[rev(seq_along(combos))]
  conda_locations <- unlist(.mapply(paste0, combos, NULL))
```
Alternatively, allow option to symlink from `/opt/homebrew/miniforge` to `/opt/miniforge` or alert user that they should do so if such installation path is detected.

title: Int64 pandas$read_parquet leads to corrupt data frame
description:
Reading a parquet file via ` pandas$read_parquet` that has a data type `Int64` (Capital i), leads to a corrupt data frame.

Info on `Int64`: https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/user_guide/integer_na.html

Similar/Related to:  https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/issues/389 

Reproducible example:

Python 3.9.7, pandas==1.3.4, under Mac OS Big Sur
The same under pandas==1.3.3. under Ubuntu.

python:
```
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame(data={'a':[1, 3]})
df["a"] = df["a"].astype('Int64')
df.to_parquet("test.parquet")
```

R:
```
> library(reticulate) 
> use_python(Sys.getenv("python_loc"))
> pandas <- import("pandas")
> pandas$read_parquet("test.parquet")
                              a
1 <environment: 0x7ff10ea89080>
2                          <NA>
Warning message:
In format.data.frame(if (omit) x[seq_len(n0), , drop = FALSE] else x,  :
  corrupt data frame: columns will be truncated or padded with NAs
```

Read in python itself:
```
>>> pd.read_parquet("test.parquet")
   a
0  1

title: py_to_r can't handle DataFrames indexed by DatetimeIndexes with milliseconds
description:
<!--
When filing a bug report, please provide a reproducible example if at all possible. This implies providing a snippet of R and / or Python code that we can copy, paste, and run to immediately observe the issue. If this is not possible, then please provide as much detail as possible to assist us in reproducing the issue locally. The output of utils::sessionInfo() and reticulate::py_config() will often be helpful.

If your issue is not reproducible, it is unlikely that we will be able to help.
-->

To reproduce the error, I created a Python script called "millisecond_index.py" containing:
```python
import pandas as pd

foo = pd.DataFrame(range(5), columns=["a"])
foo.index = pd.date_range("1970-01-01", periods=5, freq="1ms")
```

Then from R I called `reticulate::source_python("millisecond_index.py")`.

I got the error: 

> Error in `.rowNamesDF<-`(x, value = value) : 
>   duplicate 'row.names' are not allowed
> In addition: Warning message:
> non-unique value when setting 'row.names': ‘1970-01-01 00:00:00’ 

I traced the issue to [conversion.R:378](https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/a3725fd738ce9f9c027640c3a8262643170e41b2/R/conversion.R#L378), where `row.names` is set to the `POSIXct` version of the `DatetimeIndex`. You can reproduce the error in just R with:

``` r
foo <- data.frame(a = 1:5)
index <- as.POSIXct("1970-01-01") + (0:4) / 1000
row.names(foo) <- index
#> Warning: non-unique value when setting 'row.names': '1970-01-01 00:00:00'
#> Error in `.rowNamesDF<-`(x, value = value): duplicate 'row.names' are not allowed
```

<sup>Created on 2021-10-05 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.0)</sup>

I think a potential fix is to first convert the `POSIXct` vector to ISO format before setting the row names.

title: `import_from_path()` with `delay_load = TRUE` fails
description:
`import_from_path()` with `delay_load = TRUE` fails;

```R
modules_path <- system.file("python", package = package)
anonymize <<- reticulate::import_from_path(
    "anonymize",
    modules_path,
    delay_load = TRUE
)
```

leads to an error;
```
 Error: $ operator is invalid for atomic vectors 
3. delay_load$before_load %||% function() {} 
2. import_from_path_delayed(module, path, convert, delay_load) 
1. reticulate::import_from_path("anonymize", modules_path, delay_load = TRUE)
```

Because `reticulate:::import_from_path_delayed()` assumes `delay_load` to be a list. The documentation for the `import_` class of functions specifically states that `delay_load = TRUE` is "normally the right choice", and in fact specifically gives an example that will fail: 
```R
reticulate::import_from_path(<module>, path = path, delay_load = TRUE)
```

title: Consider exporting `conda_list_packages()`
description:
I was in the midst of writing a function to perform exactly this when I stumbled upon the internal reticulate function [`conda_list_packages()`](https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/577acd2dfd43b48720037eb0851f20e377dbb802/R/conda.R#L530).

This is a very useful function to have, both as a reticulate user and as a developer. Brian

title: reticulate::conda_install(pip=TRUE) broken for 1.21
description:
With the recently-released reticulate 1.21, `conda_install` fails if pip=TRUE e.g.

```r
install.packages('reticulate')
reticulate::conda_create("r-test-broken", packages=c('python=3.8'))
reticulate::conda_install("tqdm", pip=TRUE, envname="r-test-broken")
```
returns the error: 

```r
Error in conda_dll_paths() : conda environment r-reticulate not found
```

with traceback

```
4: stop("conda environment ", envname, " not found")
3: conda_dll_paths()
2: pip_install(python = python, packages = packages, pip_options = pip_options,
       ignore_installed = pip_ignore_installed)
1: reticulate::conda_install("tqdm", pip = TRUE, envname = "r-test-broken")
```

AFAICT, the issue is that  1.21 adds a call to [conda_dll_paths](https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/e48fb8cf09989fe7c3e7e708ece4058fdfd7cbfa/R/conda.R#L403) in [pip_install](https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/e48fb8cf09989fe7c3e7e708ece4058fdfd7cbfa/R/pip.R#L33), without passing the environment name, so it ultimately falls back to the [default](https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/4967abddb35865a1be6ad839298695f1481bcade/R/python-environments.R#L5) case of python_environment_resolve, which reports ‘r-reticulate’ unless the user has set RETICULATE_PYTHON_ENV.  That environment is not guaranteed to exist, so the following subset returns a 0-row data frame and falls back to the 'environment not found' error condition.

I'm not close enough to reticulate's development to know the right fix, but seems like, at least, pip_install should take an envname to pass to conda_dll_paths, and conda_install should provide the env set by the user?

title: Redirected output from reticulate is not shown in Jupyter
description:
Standard output from Python when invoked by reticulate is not shown by the R kernel in Jupyter Notebooks. This is problematic, because we can't show progress for long running commands.

We can work around this – and show all the output in the end – by specifically capturing the standard output rather than just redirecting with reticulate. However, this still does not allow us to show progress.

It looks like it stems from this Rprintf call: https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/4967abddb35865a1be6ad839298695f1481bcade/src/output.cpp#L8

Which was introduced a few years ago in this commit: https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/commit/672f20a1b66873d75f238e250ae5f62d6f9f999d

And it doesn't print, presumably because non-R stdout/stderr is not captured by Jupyter:
https://github.com/IRkernel/IRkernel/issues/416

We'll submit a patch for this shortly, but I'm not sure what the best approach is. We could:
- Default write using R (this would break terminal control sequences)
- Allow the user to specify their desired output
- Check manually for the context in which we're operating, and redirect appropriately (ala https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/4967abddb35865a1be6ad839298695f1481bcade/R/output.R#L8)

Any preference or other ideas?

title: passing env from R to python
description:
Having resolved my installation of mosek problem, I'm now stymied by a lack of understanding of how to pass environments from R to python.  I'm calling a python function to do regularized logistic regression, the call looks like this:
logisticRegression(env, X, y, lambda).  In the original python code there was a "env = Env()" line and that seemed to do the necessary initialization.  Including this line and using source_python("LRL.py") produces a message that Env isn't defined. And various attempts to substitute R objects for env in an R call have all failed.  Any guidance would be much appreciated.

import mosek
from mosek import *
import numpy as np 
import sys, itertools

#env = Env()
inf = 0.0

# t_i >= log( 1 + exp(u_i) ), i = 0..n-1
# Adds auxiliary variables and constraints
def softplus(task, t, u, n):
    nvar = task.getnumvar()
    ncon = task.getnumcon()
    task.appendvars(6*n)
    task.appendcons(3*n)
    z1, z2, v1, v2, q1, q2 = nvar, nvar+n, nvar+2*n, nvar+3*n, nvar+4*n, nvar+5*n
    zcon, v1con, v2con = ncon, ncon+n, ncon+2*n

    # z1 + z2 = 1
    task.putaijlist(range(zcon, zcon+n), range(z1, z1+n), [1]*n)
    task.putaijlist(range(zcon, zcon+n), range(z2, z2+n), [1]*n)
    # u - t - v1 = 0
    task.putaijlist(range(v1con, v1con+n), range(u, u+n), [1]*n)
    task.putaijlist(range(v1con, v1con+n), range(t, t+n), [-1]*n)
    task.putaijlist(range(v1con, v1con+n), range(v1, v1+n), [-1]*n)
    # - t - v2 = 0
    task.putaijlist(range(v2con, v2con+n), range(t, t+n), [-1]*n)
    task.putaijlist(range(v2con, v2con+n), range(v2, v2+n), [-1]*n)
    # Bounds for all constraints
    task.putconboundslice(ncon, ncon+3*n, [boundkey.fx]*(3*n), [1]*n+[0]*(2*n), [1]*n+[0]*(2*n))
    # Bounds for variables
    task.putvarboundsliceconst(nvar, nvar+4*n, boundkey.fr, -inf, inf)
    task.putvarboundsliceconst(nvar+4*n, nvar+6*n, boundkey.fx, 1, 1)

    # Cones
    for i in range(n):
        task.appendcone(conetype.pexp, 0.0, [z1+i, q1+i, v1+i])
        task.appendcone(conetype.pexp, 0.0, [z2+i, q2+i, v2+i])


# Model logistic regression (regularized with full 2-norm of theta)
# X - n x d matrix of data points
# y - length n vector classifying training points
# lamb - regularization parameter
def logisticRegression(env, X, y, lamb=1.0):
    n, d = int(X.shape[0]), int(X.shape[1])         # num samples, dimension
    
    with env.Task() as task:
        # Variables [r; theta; t; u]
        nvar = 1+d+2*n
        task.appendvars(nvar)
        task.putvarboundsliceconst(0, nvar, boundkey.fr, -inf, inf)
        r, theta, t, u, = 0, 1, 1+d, 1+d+n
        
        # Constraints: theta'*X +/- u = 0
        task.appendcons(n)
        task.putconboundsliceconst(0, n, boundkey.fx, 0.0, 0.0)            

        # Objective lambda*r + sum(t)
        task.putcj(r, lamb)
        task.putclist(range(t, t+n), [1.0]*n)

        # The X block in theta'*X +/- u = 0
        uCoeff = []
        for i in range(n):
            task.putaijlist([i]*d, range(theta, theta+d), X[i])
            uCoeff.append(1 if y[i] == 1 else -1)
        # +/- coefficients in u depending on y
        task.putaijlist(range(n), range(u, u+n), uCoeff)

        # Softplus function constraints
        softplus(task, t, u, n)

        # Regularization l2 -> l1
        #task.appendconeseq(conetype.quad, 0.0, 1+d, r)
        task.appendconesseq([conetype.quad]*(1+d), [0.0]*(1+d), [2]*(1+d), r)

        # Solution
        task.optimize()
        xx = [0.0]*d
        task.getxxslice(soltype.itr, theta, theta+d, xx)

        return xx

title: reticulate in rstudio server doesn't inherit environment variables--allow a workaround to set environment variables
description:
Setting PYTHONUSERBASE and PYTHONPATH variables affects the behavior of where modules are imported from for the normal python shell, but via reticulate in rstudio server these variables are not inherited. This can be a problem since it causes rstudio server reticulate to behave abnormally/unexpectedly with respect to other ways of calling python.

 This is more of an rstudio server issue (because rstudio server doesn't inherit R-related environment variables either without IT admin intervention at startup via PAM or systemd) but it's particularly a problem for non-root users (ie using an already-started rstudio server instance) when using reticulate.  Normal users can set R environment variables using standard R methods (.Renviron, .Rprofile), but setting environment variables for python in these files doesn't seem to work. 

I don't know what the best solution here is, but here are a few ideas:
- have reticulate source .Renviron prior to starting the python interpreter
- have reticulate source a separate user-defined file to source prior to starting the python interpreter

Either of these would allow making reticulate's behavior in Rstudio server closer to the normal python behavior (albeit as manual workaround).

title: NAs coerced to character when dataframe is an attribute of a class
description:
I'm using reticulate to interact with an instance of a Python class. One attribute of that class is a dataframe. When I clean that dataframe up, it looks as I expect. However, when I attempt to assign the cleaned version back to the attribute, the `NA` values get converted to `"NA"` strings. I've played around with this quite a bit but I'm still not sure whether this is a bug or something I'm doing wrong. Any advice would be much appreciated – thank you!

## Reproducible Example
```r
library(reticulate)

# Create an instance of a Python class
# with a dataframe containing `None` as an attribute
py_string <- "
import pandas as pd

class MyClass:
  def __init__(self, df):
    self.df = df

my_class = MyClass(pd.DataFrame({'x': [None, 'abc']}))"

reticulate::py_run_string(py_string)

# The None value results in the column being read in as a list
any(sapply(py$my_class$df, class) == "list")
# > [1] TRUE

# So we un-list it
clean_df <- tidyr::unnest(py$my_class$df, 1, keep_empty = TRUE)

# Assign the cleaned dataframe back to the `df` attribute of this class
py$my_class$df <- clean_df

# We no longer have a list column (good !)
any(sapply(py$my_class$df, class) == "list")
# > [1] FALSE

# But the NA value is getting coverted to a string (bad !)
# The cleaned dataframe has one NA (correct)
# The attribute does not (because the NA turned into string "NA")
sum(is.na(clean_df$x)) == sum(is.na(py$my_class$df))
# > [1] FALSE

# Setting the attribute with py_set_attr also doesn't work
reticulate::py_set_attr(py$my_class, "df", clean_df)
sum(is.na(clean_df$x)) == sum(is.na(py$my_class$df))
# > [1] FALSE
```

title: Simplification of python lists
description:
Hello. I'm working on improving the experience around subclassing python classes from R. Subclassing is a design pattern heavily encouraged in the python keras/tensorflow api, and I think it's important to enable similar usage on the R side.

One of the issues I'm encountering is due to automatic simplification of python lists.
User supplied R lists convert to python lists, but then they don't convert back to R lists.

### Where it comes up

In python it's common to do:
```python
class MyLayer(keras.layers.Layer):
  def __init__(self, **kwargs):
    super().__init__(**kwargs)
    
my_layer = MyLayer(input_shape = [32])
```

In R, I want users to be able to do the equivalent:

(for the moment, please ignore the R syntax for constructing and instantiating
classes and resolving `super`, I intend to open a separate discussion/PR for that soon)

```r
MyLayer <- r_to_py(R6Class("MyLayer",
  inherit = keras$layers$Layer,
  public = list(
    `__init__` = function(self, ...) {
      super$`__init__`(...)
    }
  )
))

my_layer <- MyLayer(input_shape = shape(32))
```

In the above R example, the issue I'm encountering is that arguments supplied to
`...` are converted between python and R multiple times, Concretely, they :

- start as R objects, 
- convert to python objects (for `MyLayer.__new__()`), 
- convert back to R objects (for `MyLayer.__init__()`), 
- convert back again to python objects (for `super().__init__()`). 

In the process, what the caller intended to be a list gets simplified to a scalar:
(R) `shape(32)` -> (py) `[32]` -> (R) `c(32)` -> (py) `32`, resulting in an exception from `keras.layers.Layer.__init__`.

Note, this doesn't just come up when passing R `...` from one python function to another. Because `self` is a python object, the potential for unintended simplification is present anytime `self` has an attribute set and then accessed. For example, another common pattern in keras custom layers is to defer building a layer's weights by providing a `build` method:

```r
MyLayer <- r_to_py(R6Class("MyLayer",
  inherit = keras$layers$Layer,
  public = list(
    `__init__` = function(self, weight_shape, ...) {
      super$`__init__`(...)
      self$weight_shape <- weight_shape
    },
    build = function(self, input_shape) {
      self$custom_weight <- super$add_weight(
        shape = self$weight_shape
      )
      super$build(input_shape)
    }
  )
))

my_layer <- MyLayer()
input <- layer_input(shape(10))
my_layer(input) 
```

This also throws an exception, because the value supplied to `weight_shape` is converted to a python list on assignment to `self$input_shape`, simplified to an R numeric when it's accessed in `build`, and then converted to a python scalar when passed on to `super$add_weight()`.

I can try to "fix-up" specific keywords I know about in advance like this in keras, but I wonder if there is perhaps a more sustainable solution that allows for lossless conversion for more objects crossing the R <--> py boundary multiple times.

### Some ideas for how to resolve this (in order of most-to-least disruptive)

1) Disable auto-simplification of python lists to R vectors; python lists always get converted to R lists. This is probably too disruptive a change at this point, so maybe it's off the table, but IMO this is the cleanest resolution. Just to go through the thought exercise, this is what the new conversion behavior could be: 
```
R          ->       py      ->      R            lossless
---------------------------------------------------------
1                    1              1               yes
c(1,2)            [1,2]         list(1,2)           no
list(1)             [1]         list(1)             yes
list(1,2)         [1,2]         list(1,2)           yes
array(c(1))    np.array([1])    array(c(1))         yes
array(c(1,2))  np.array([1,2])  array(c(1,2))       yes
```

In slack @dfalbel made an excellent suggestion: to assist with the transition we could provide a context switch for users with code that depends on the automatic simplification `with_old_conversion_behavior({})`.


2) Add a dummy python class: 
  ```python
  class Rlist(list): pass
  ```
  Objects that originate as R lists get converted to python's `Rlist`. The `Rlist` behaves exactly like a builtin python list, but on the way back to R we do the equivalent of `py_to_r.rpytools.rtypes.Rlist <- function(x) as.list(NextMethod())`.

3) Introduce a breaking change by changing `tensorflow::shape` to return a `tf$TensorShape()` object. This solves the roundtrip issue, but breaks any code that manipulates the shape where an R list is expected. We could help lessen the impact by providing `c`, `[`, `[[`, `[<-`, and `[[<-` S3 methods for `tf.TensorShape` objects.

4) Do the equivalent of (2), but confined to just the R lists returned by `tensorflow::shape`. This would probably mean making the return object from `shape` an S3 class with `c`, `[`, `[[`, `[<-`, and `[[<-`, and `r_to_py` methods, and then a companion `py_to_r` method.

5) Leave `tensorflow::shape()` as-is. Do the equivalent of (3) but in new function `tf_shape`. Update all docs/tutorials/unittests to swap `shape` for `tf_shape()`.

Objects round-tripping between python-land and R-land is going to be pretty unavoidable, and requiring the user to "fix-up" those objects every time with `as.list()` seems cumbersome, especially if it means objects have to be broken out of `...` to do so.

Here is a minimal example demonstrating simplification:
```r
py_reflect <- reticulate::py_run_string(
"def reflect(x):
  print('python fn received: ', x)
  return x
")$reflect
list()    |> py_reflect() |> py_reflect()   # ok     
list(1,2) |> py_reflect() |> py_reflect()   # not ideal, but not my main issue  
list(1)   |> py_reflect() |> py_reflect()   # my main issue
```
giving output:
```r
> list()    |> py_reflect() |> py_reflect()   # ok     
list()
python fn received:  []
python fn received:  []
> list(1,2) |> py_reflect() |> py_reflect()   # not ideal, but not my main issue  
[1] 1 2
python fn received:  [1.0, 2.0]
python fn received:  [1.0, 2.0]
> list(1)   |> py_reflect() |> py_reflect()   # my main issue
[1] 1
python fn received:  [1.0]
python fn received:  1.0
```

After writing this out, I'm on the fence between options (1) or (5), perhaps with a small preference for (1). I would be curious to hear your thoughts.
@kevinushey @dfalbel @skeydan

title: Terminal `with` blocks do not execute in Rmd
description:
A terminal Python `with` block in a cell appears to confuse the Rmd cell executor. For example, with the following cell content:

    ```{python}
    with open("/tmp/beebop", "w") as f:
      f.write("abc")

>>> with open("/tmp/beebop", "w") as f:

... 
```

whereas

    ```{python}
    with open("/tmp/beebop", "w") as f:

title: questions about use_condaenv() and whether or not its safe to use the full conda environment?
description:
Hi, 

So a number of us have noticed that after we call use_condaenv(), we get access not only to the python that is present in that environment, but ALSO access to anything custom from the local command line (providing that we 1st activate that python so that it gets lazily bound to our session).

And: this is actually extremely powerful.  Because it means that we can install CLI tools into conda environments and then get access to them from RStudio notebooks.  We can run some R code, then process a file using anything that runs in linux, and then have another step that continues from that point on...  etc.

BUT: there are some things that lead me to think that this is awesomeness is actually an accidental 'side effect' of how reticulate is binding python.  For one thing, I cannot ever let go of an environment once I have bound it onto a specific python.  After I have called both use_condaenv() and anything from python, there does not seem to be any way to tell reticulate to 'let go' so that I could attach a different environment later on in my notebook.  And the other issue is (of course), that I have no way to sidestep the lazy binding mechanic for Python.  IOW, when using this "feature", I normally want to just tell the session that I am both keen to us the environment and ALSO that I mean it in one command.   Currently, have to both indicate that I want the environment using use_condaenv() and then separately also call some python code before I can get access to the other stuff in the environment.   The fact that this is inconvenient like this seems like a big hint that only Python was intended to be supported in this way.  And it also suggests that by using this "feature" I might be asking for trouble down the road...

But if I am right and this was not the intention.  Then I have to say that this more limited design seems unambitious.  The real world of data science is really MUCH bigger than just R and python.  So here are my questions: 

1) Am I right about this "feature" being just an accidental side effect?
2) If I am right about that, is there any chance you guys might embrace making this a real feature?
3) What should I tell all the people that I know who want to use this "feature"?  Should I just them to stop using RStudio and instead look more closely at toolchains like SoS?  Or are you guys already thinking about supporting it?

I know that you guys are probably always busy.  But it seems like this might be an opportunity to reach a much wider audience.  You currently have a MUCH nicer IDE than tools like Jupyter are providing.  So I don't want to migrate/train people away from it if we don't have to.  But people also need to be able to use a greater diversity of tools.

Curious to hear your thoughts.


Cheers,

  Marc

title: Support for pipenv?
description:
Would your team consider implementing more direct support for users using `pipenv` to manage the python environment?  

[Pipenv](https://github.com/pypa/pipenv) is a widely used approach maintained by the Python Packaging Authority, PyPa, for managing virtualenvs for different projects automatically by using a simple `Pipfile` in the project directory.  It is built on the virutalenv system, so we can still access pipenv environments with `reticulate` already, but it is cumbersome and lacks the syncing features we get from using pipenv directly, such as:

- You no longer need to use pip and virtualenv separately. They work together.
- Managing a requirements.txt file can be [problematic](https://kenreitz.org/essays/2016/02/25/a-better-pip-workflow)
- Hashes are used everywhere, always. Security. Automatically expose security vulnerabilities.

- pipenv also lets us install & switch between different python versions via pyenv, and a given project can be set to use a specific python version easily.

I know this also overlaps a bit with your `renv` package, and I'd be happy to transfer this issue there if you think that's better.  In general I think `pipenv` approach with a `Pipfile` is very much in the same spirit as `renv`, and is a bit cleaner way to do what `renv` tries to do with regards to python via `requirements.txt`.  Another nice feature of the `pipenv` approach is that you have consistent behavior in 'pure python' in the project, which automatically loads the Pipenv file, as you would in the R environment, instead of having to manually do something like `source renv/python/bin/activate` in the shell to make renv's python env accessible on the terminal.  Anyway I think @kevinushey would like `pipenv` and so just wanted to toss it out there!

title: With reticulate, xgboost with certain type of hyperparameters cannot be paralleled.
description:
I am building a random forest via xgboost following the instruction at https://xgboost.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorials/rf.html. The R codes are like below (using the sample from the library xgboost) :

data(agaricus.train, package='xgboost')
data(agaricus.test, package='xgboost')
train <- agaricus.train
test <- agaricus.test
random.forest.model<- xgboost(data = train$data, label = train$label, max_depth = 6,
eta = 1, nthread = 5, nrounds = 1, objective = "binary:logistic", num_parallel_tree = 10000)

When running the codes above in RStudio directly, from the backend of the server (centos Linux) I can see that five CPUs are activated and used for the model.

However, when I run the python equivalent in RStudio via reticulate, no matter how I set nthread, only one CPU is active and used, indicating that the process becomes single-threaded.

 param = {'max_depth': 6, 
                 'eta': 1,
                  'nthread': 5,
                   'num_parallel_tree': 10000,
                   'objective': 'binary:logistic'}

random_forest_model = xgb.train(param, dtrain, num_round=1)

Moreover, the python codes above can be run in parallel using Jupyter with no issue.  In addition, for a 'traditional' xgboost with multiple rounds, there is no such issue in reticulate.

Any ideas? The process takes a lot of time after becoming single-threaded, which is very unfavorable for my work.

Thank you.

---

library(reticulate)

```


```{python setup, cache=FALSE, message = FALSE, eval=TRUE}
import pandas as pd
import altair as alt
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

flights_url = "https://github.com/byuidatascience/data4python4ds/raw/master/data-raw/flights/flights.csv"

flights

title: "OSError: [Errno 40] Too many levels of symbolic links" on ncurses-6.2 when installing r-miniconda.
description:
Hi,

A few users of our RStudio Server Pro (served on VMs) has an issue when they install the r-miniconda with the "reticulate::install_miniconda()" function. I tried to reproduce the problem and I get the same error.

The steps to reproduce it on RStudio are:

- install.packages('reticulate')
- reticulate::install_miniconda()

The issue occurs when the installation creates automatically a conda environment called "r-reticulate" and try to install the python packages specified as a parameter on "conda_create(...)". It seems that one of the packages, ncurses-6.2, generates a file in the path "/home/<my_user>/.local/share/r-miniconda/pkgs/ncurses-6.2-h58526e2_4/share/terminfo/N/NCR260VT300WPP" that contains a loop of symlinks that are pointing to himself. I think that this is the reason when the installation is verifying the transaction, then fails and throws the "OSError: [Errno 40] Too many levels of symbolic links: '/home/<my_user>/.local/share/r-miniconda/pkgs/ncurses-6.2-h58526e2_4/share/terminfo/N/NCR260VT300WPP'".

With this issue/bug it can't be able to create the environment correctly on a default behaviour of the RStudio and the reticulate package.

To look at the symlinks on a terminal I used the following command:
"namei -l /home/<my_user>/.local/share/r-miniconda/pkgs/ncurses-6.2-h58526e2_4/share/terminfo/N/NCR260VT300WPP"

title: Need to call ensurepip in new Python environments.
description:
I was running into a confusing problem installing a package into a fresh version of reticulate.  Here is the 
code snippet that generated the error:
```
library(reticulate)
if (length(virtualenv_list()) == 0L) virtualenv_create()
use_virtualenv("r-reticulate")

virtualenv_install("r-reticulate","pomegranate")
pom <- import("pomegranate")
```
It is probably important that I have never used the r-reticulate before, so it has no packages installed, including pip.
I got the following mysterious error messages:
```
> virtualenv_install("r-reticulate","pomegranate")
+ 
Using virtual environment 'r-reticulate' ...
Error: invalid version specification ‘’, ‘  ’
In addition: Warning messages:
1: In system2(python, c("-c", shQuote(command)), stdout = TRUE, stderr = TRUE) :
  running command ''/home/ralmond/.virtualenvs/r-reticulate/bin/python' -c 'import sys; import pip; sys.stdout.write(pip.__version__)' 2>&1' had status 1
2: In if (idx != -1) version <- substring(version, 1, idx - 1) :
  the condition has length > 1 and only the first element will be used
```
A bit of work in the console determined that the problem is that pip is not installed into the .virtualenv version of python.
```
ralmond@cherry:~$ .virtualenvs/r-reticulate/bin/python -c 'import sys; import pip; sys.stdout.wirte(pip.__version__)'
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 1, in <module>
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pip'

Good news is that calling
Calling `.virtualenvs/r-reticulate/bin/python -m ensurepip` solved the problem.  This needs to be put into the `virtualenv_create()` function or maybe `virtual_install()`.

# Load Packages
import numpy as np

```

title: Better documentation of use_python, use_condaenv, use_miniconda
description:
It's not clear how conda_create() selects version number currently, but it seems like there's no way to specify it. The conda CLI to creating a new environment allows specification of the exact version of python.  This means you need to resort to using the CLI if you want to control what version of python gets put into the environment.

Additionally, this documentation should make it more clear that if you're creating a conda environment, you want use_python to point to the python binary inside the conda environment. Results are ... unpredictable if you try to point to a python version that's not in the conda environment (i think the python version basically gets silently ignored). That a conda environment has its own python binary may be obvious to people who are familiar with conda environments, but it wasn't clear from the reticulate documentation on using conda. I think the fact that I couldn't specify a python version in conda_create() contributed to my confusion, so clearer documentationn around this would help others in the future.

EDIT: see additional suggestions for improving documentation in this [comment](https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/issues/949#issuecomment-775421575):

title: Better documentation for environment variables
description:
RETICULATE_PYTHON must point to a binary
RETICULATE_MINICONDA_PATH needs to point to a directory *and not the binary*

I only figured this out by reading the source code after getting errors. This should be better documented. Thanks!

I'm wondering if there is an easy way to list the Python Packages that are in a specific python environment. Something like `conda_list()` but for path packages within an environment. 

My current process is to head over to the terminal, activate a conda environment with `conda activate my_env` then use `conda list -n my_env`.

Seems like it would be a useful function if available.

title: Avoid installation of ceratin python packages
description:
Is there any way to avoid installation of particular python packages using reticulate? 
For instance, is there any way to repeat this piece of python code: 
`virtualenv -p /usr/bin/python3 venv/py3 --verbose --no-setuptools`

Something like:
`reticulate::virtualenv_create("myenv", python="/usr/bin/python3", packages =  c("no-setuptools"))`

title: Avoid invoking miniconda_install_prompt when a Python PATH is not found
description:
First off, thanks for the development of this amazing package :clap:  :clap:. **[rgee](https://github.com/r-spatial/rgee)** will not exist without reticulate :).

Would be possible that in future releases of **reticulate**, **py_available**, returns FALSE instead of  [miniconda_install_prompt](https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/9be9bd0477ae37503bafeecb1406bb60a5ea728f/R/config.R#L182) when users do not count with a Python Path. Something like this would be perfect:

```r
reticulate::py_available(initialize = TRUE, miniconda_install=FALSE)
#> FALSE
```
This would help me a lot to correctly display help messages inside rgee. Does this has sense?. I would be happy to work in the PR :)

title: BLAS compatiblity issue
description:
I recently stumbled across a BLAS compatiblity issue. Although this issue may only occur seldomly (depending on your system's and `numpy`'s BLAS version), I wanted to report/discuss it nevertheless.

First some information about my setup:

```
5.10.7-arch1-1

R version 4.0.3 (2020-10-10)
Platform: x86_64-pc-linux-gnu (64-bit)
Running under: Arch Linux

Matrix products: default
BLAS:   /usr/lib/libopenblasp-r0.3.13.so
LAPACK: /usr/lib/liblapack.so.3.9.0

reticulate_1.18
```


```r
library(reticulate)
py_config()
```

```
python:         /home/lps/.local/share/r-miniconda/envs/r-reticulate/bin/python
libpython:      /home/lps/.local/share/r-miniconda/envs/r-reticulate/lib/libpython3.6m.so
pythonhome:     /home/lps/.local/share/r-miniconda/envs/r-reticulate:/home/lps/.local/share/r-miniconda/envs/r-reticulate
version:        3.6.10 |Anaconda, Inc.| (default, Mar 25 2020, 23:51:54)  [GCC 7.3.0]
numpy:          /home/lps/.local/share/r-miniconda/envs/r-reticulate/lib/python3.6/site-packages/numpy
numpy_version:  1.19.4
```

Now, suppose I want to invert a matrix in `R` using `numpy` via `reticulate`:

```r
py_run_string("import numpy as np")
py_run_string("from numpy.linalg import inv")
py_run_string("a = np.array([[1., 2., -3., -1.], [3., -4., 5., 1.], [1., 2., 3., -10.], [15., 2., -3., -1.]])")
py_run_string("inv(a)")
```

This gives me a segfault:

```
 *** caught segfault ***
address (nil), cause 'memory not mapped'

Traceback:
 1: py_run_string_impl(code, local, convert)
 2: py_run_string("inv(a)")

Possible actions:
1: abort (with core dump, if enabled)
2: normal R exit
3: exit R without saving workspace
4: exit R saving workspace
Selection:
```

Debugging via `R -d gdb --vanilla` yields:
```
py_run_string("inv(a)")
Thread 1 "R" received signal SIGSEGV, Segmentation fault.
0x00007ffff6e299a4 in drot_k_SANDYBRIDGE () from /usr/lib/libblas.so.3
(gdb) where
#0  0x00007ffff6e299a4 in drot_k_SANDYBRIDGE () from /usr/lib/libblas.so.3
#1  0x00007fffcbc84e4d in dgetf2_k ()
   from /home/lps/.local/share/r-miniconda/envs/r-reticulate/lib/python3.6/site-packages/numpy/core/../../numpy.libs/libopenblasp-r0-ae94cfde.3.9.dev.so
#2  0x00007fffcbc80b31 in dgetrf_parallel ()
   from /home/lps/.local/share/r-miniconda/envs/r-reticulate/lib/python3.6/site-packages/numpy/core/../../numpy.libs/libopenblasp-r0-ae94cfde.3.9.dev.so
#3  0x00007fffcba746a9 in dgesv_ ()
   from /home/lps/.local/share/r-miniconda/envs/r-reticulate/lib/python3.6/site-packages/numpy/core/../../numpy.libs/libopenblasp-r0-ae94cfde.3.9.dev.so
#4  0x00007fffca56f313 in DOUBLE_inv ()
   from /home/lps/.local/share/r-miniconda/envs/r-reticulate/lib/python3.6/site-packages/numpy/linalg/_umath_linalg.cpython-36m-x86_64-linux-gnu.so
#5  0x00007fffcd9add6b in PyUFunc_GenericFunction_int ()
   from /home/lps/.local/share/r-miniconda/envs/r-reticulate/lib/python3.6/site-packages/numpy/core/_multiarray_umath.cpython-36m-x86_64-linux-gnu.so
#6  0x00007fffcd9ae276 in ufunc_generic_call ()
   from /home/lps/.local/share/r-miniconda/envs/r-reticulate/lib/python3.6/site-packages/numpy/core/_multiarray_umath.cpython-36m-x86_64-linux-gnu.so
.
.
.
```

Note that `/usr/lib/libblas.so.3` is a symlink to
```
readlink -f /usr/lib/libblas.so.3/
usr/lib/libopenblasp-r0.3.13.so
```

Notably `drot_k_SANDYBRIDGE ()` actually should not be called here. I believe this is a result of `numpy` being built against a different openblas version, namely `libopenblasp-r0-ae94cfde.3.9.dev.so` whereas `R` is built against the newer `libopenblasp-r0.3.13.so`. Therefore, I believe some table lookup or something related fails, causing the segfault.

In `python` (`/home/lps/.local/share/r-miniconda/envs/r-reticulate/bin/python`) everything works as expected:
```python
import numpy as np
print(np.__file__)
```

```
/home/lps/.local/share/r-miniconda/envs/r-reticulate/lib/python3.6/site-packages/numpy/__init__.py
```

```python
from numpy.linalg import inv
a = np.array([[1., 2., -3., -1.], [3., -4., 5., 1.], [1., 2., 3., -10.], [15., 2., -3., -1.]])
inv(a)
```

```
array([[-0.07142857,  0.        ,  0.        ,  0.07142857],
       [-2.12380952, -1.1       ,  0.06666667,  0.35714286],
       [-1.48095238, -0.6       ,  0.06666667,  0.21428571],
       [-0.87619048, -0.4       , -0.06666667,  0.14285714]])
```

If I downgrade my systems openblas version to e.g., `0.3.10` or `0.3.9` the matrix inversion now also works in `R` using `numpy` via `reticulate`.

I am not sure how a good solution to this problem could look like. I guess you cannot expect different BLAS versions to be fully compatible with each other.

title: Support miniforge helpers
description:
[Miniforge](https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/) is a minimal installer for `conda`, maintained by the [`conda-forge`](https://conda-forge.org/#about) organization and sponsored by NumFOCUS, which is community-led, sets `conda-forge` as the default channel, and notably supports ARMv8 64-bit (aarch64), which may be helpful for users with M1 Macs.

I confirmed that `use_condaenv()` works with miniforge installed using Homebrew. Would you consider building helper functions for miniforge similar to those for miniconda? (e.g., `install_miniforge()`, `miniforge_path()`, `miniforge_update()`, and `use_miniforge()`?)

title: _import_hook failure when loading module via import_from_path
description:
This is somewhat tricky, so I'll try to explain it as clearly as possible, and to help an example package that has this error is available [here](https://github.com/mmuurr/sqlparse-R-package) for testing.

The package linked-to above has a very small and simple structure:
```
R/zzz.R
inst/python/sqlparse/...
```
`inst/python/sqlparse` is a Python module (version-pinned to a few years back for compatibility with Python 2.x, since that's still the version distributed by default on most OSes).
`zzz.R` contains an `.onLoad()` hook that loads the aforementioned module via `import_from_path()` and then adds each top-level module object to the package namespace; effectively an automated way to 'mimic' the Python module's namespace.

[Here's that `.onLoad()` function](https://github.com/mmuurr/sqlparse-R-package/blob/master/R/zzz.R#L1):
```r
.onLoad <- function(libname, pkgname) {
    pkg_ns_env <- parent.env(environment())
    sqlparse <- reticulate::import_from_path("sqlparse", system.file("python", "sqlparse", package = pkgname, mustWork = TRUE))
    lapply(names(sqlparse), function(name) assign(name, sqlparse[[name]], pkg_ns_env))
}
```

In the current dev version of reticulate, when I try to build or load the R package, I receive the following error (preceded here by a successful `py_config()` call to help with debugging):
```r
reticulate::py_config()
# python:         /usr/bin/python
# libpython:      /System/Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/2.7/lib/python2.7/config/libpython2.7.dylib
# pythonhome:     /System/Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/2.7:/System/Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/2.7
# version:        2.7.16 (default, Dec 13 2019, 18:00:32)  [GCC 4.2.1 Compatible Apple LLVM 11.0.0 (clang-1100.0.32.4) (-macos10.15-objc-s
# numpy:          /System/Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/2.7/Extras/lib/python/numpy
# numpy_version:  1.8.0
#
# python versions found:
# /usr/bin/python3
# /usr/bin/python

library(sqlparse)
# Error: package or namespace load failed for ‘sqlparse’:
#  .onLoad failed in loadNamespace() for 'sqlparse', details:
#   call: py_get_attr_types_impl(x, names, resolve_properties)
#   error: AttributeError: type object 'module' has no attribute 'cli'
#
# Detailed traceback:
#   File "/usr/local/lib/R/4.0/site-library/reticulate/python/rpytools/loader.py", line 31, in _import_hook
#     level=level
```

I can verify this was working with reticulate 1.16 (and any version prior to that from early-2018 onward). The sqlparse Python module embedded in the package does have a `cli` sub-module, and so I suspect the `_import_hook` is choking on that somehow, but I'm kind of stumped as to what might be happening here.

description:
Relevant language and package versions:
* R 4.0.3
* python 2.7.16 (Mac OS X's system default)

In a fresh R session, this has been happening to me:

reticulate::py_config()

# numpy:          /System/Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/2.7/Extras/lib/python/numpy
# numpy_version:  1.8.0

# python versions found:
# /usr/bin/python3
# /usr/bin/python
```
... i.e. on the first `py_config()` call I get an error. Making the same `py_config()` call immediately afterwards succeeds, and it appears I can load Python modules just fine. (Though I haven't yet rigorously tested Python code to make sure the Python environment is properly functioning, because of the package problem described below.)

In an interactive R session, this would be fine (if not annoying/weird), but this is suddenly breaking a package of mine where `.onLoad()` includes adding a reticulate/Python object into the package's namespace (via reticulate's `import_from_path` with some package-embedded Python code).

One could conceivably around this by ensuring a successful reticulate initialization before loading the package, but the "testing if installed package can be loaded..." phase of building/installing the package is failing (naturally), since it only knows to try to initialize reticulate once.

title: howto: capturing stdout/stderr
description:
Can R/R Markdown capture and/or display the output from a Python call like `os.system`?

Here are a number of R Markdown chunks that I have used to experiment; this is with the CRAN 1.16 version of reticulate.

First, a Python chunk:

````markdown
```{python}
import os
os.system("wheel version")
```
````

This outputs the exit code of the program and does not include the stdout/stderr in the rendered document:

```
## 0
```

Next, an R chunk using `py_capture_output`:

````markdown
```{r}
reticulate::py_capture_output('os.system("wheel version")')
```
````

This outputs an empty string:

```
## [1] ""
```

An empty string is also returned when run from the R console:

```
> reticulate::py_capture_output('os.system("wheel version")')
[1] ""
```

Next, trying to import the Python "os" module into R:

````markdown
```{r}
os <- reticulate::import("os")
os$system("wheel version")
```
````

This outputs the exit code of the program:

```
## [1] 0
```

When run from the R console, we see the program output, but it is not captured:

```
> os$system("wheel version")
wheel 0.33.1
[1] 0
```

Here is an R chunk using the R `system` function and its `intern` argument:

````markdown
```{r}
system("wheel version", intern = TRUE)
```
```````

This emits the program output!

```
## [1] "wheel 0.33.1"
```

Lastly, a bash chunk:

````markdown
```{bash}
wheel version
```
````

This also emits the program output into the rendered document:

```
## wheel 0.33.1
```

title: PyClass issue
description:
Hi @kevinushey. We have ported an example from Python to R. https://keras-team.github.io/keras-tuner/tutorials/subclass-tuner/
After TensorFlow 2.2 breaking changes this example stopped working from R. My guess is the problem with reticulate::PyClass.
Could you share your opinion, please?

> I used ```reticulate::import from the path``` the python class from python side and it worked. However, it fails when I construct the class with PyClass. As you see from the output, the training runs fine but it fails with the following:

```
oracle <- kt$oracles$BayesianOptimization(
  objective=kt$Objective('loss', 'min'), # I think this fails but not sure why
  max_trials=2L)

tuner = MyTuner(
  oracle=oracle,
  hypermodel=conv_build_model,
  directory='results',
  project_name='mnist_custo1m2')
```
Python side is the same:

```
tuner = MyTuner(
      oracle=kt.oracles.BayesianOptimization(
          objective=kt.Objective('loss', 'min'),
          max_trials=2),
      hypermodel=build_model,
      directory='results',
      project_name='mnist_custom_training')
```

## R side

```
library(keras)
library(tensorflow)
library(tfdatasets)
library(reticulate)

kt = reticulate::import('kerastuner')

physical_devices = tf$config$list_physical_devices('GPU')
tf$config$experimental$set_memory_growth(physical_devices[[1]], TRUE)

conv_build_model = function(hp) {
  'Builds a convolutional model.'
  inputs = layer_input(shape=c(28, 28, 1))
  
  x = inputs
  
  for (i in 1:hp$Int('conv_layers', 1, 3, default=3)) {
    x = x %>% layer_conv_2d(filters = hp$Int(paste('filters_', i, sep = ''), 4, 32, step=4, default=8),
                            kernel_size = hp$Int(paste('kernel_size_', i, sep = ''), 3, 5),
                            activation ='relu',
                            padding='same')
    if (hp$Choice(paste('pooling', i, sep = ''), c('max', 'avg')) == 'max') {
      x = x %>% layer_max_pooling_2d()
    } else {
      x = x %>% layer_average_pooling_2d()
    }
    x = x %>% layer_batch_normalization()
    x = x %>% layer_activation_relu()
    
  }
  if (hp$Choice('global_pooling', c('max', 'avg')) == 'max') {
    x = x %>% layer_global_max_pooling_2d()
  } else {
    x = x %>% layer_global_average_pooling_2d()
  }
  
  outputs = x %>% layer_dense(10, activation='softmax')
  model = keras_model(inputs, outputs)
  optimizer = hp$Choice('optimizer', c('adam', 'sgd'))
  model %>% compile(optimizer, loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy', 
                    metrics='accuracy')
  return(model)
}

MyTuner <- reticulate::PyClass(
  'Tuner',
  inherit = kt$Tuner,
  list(
    run_trial = function(self, trial, train_ds){
      
      hp = trial$hyperparameters
      
      train_ds = train_ds %>% dataset_batch(hp$Int('batch_size', 32, 128, step=32, default=64))
      
      model = self$hypermodel$build(trial$hyperparameters)
      
      lr = hp$Float('learning_rate', 1e-4, 1e-2, sampling='log', default=1e-3)
      
      optimizer = optimizer_adam(lr)
      
      epoch_loss_metric = tf$keras$metrics$Mean(name='accuracy')
      
      
      run_train_step = function(data){
        images = data[[1]]
        labels = data[[2]]
        
        
        with (tf$GradientTape() %as% tape,{
          logits = model(images)
          loss = tf$keras$losses$sparse_categorical_crossentropy(labels, logits)
          if(length(model$losses) > 0){
            loss = loss + tf$math$add_n(model$losses)
          }
          gradients = tape$gradient(loss, model$trainable_variables)
        })
        optimizer$apply_gradients(purrr::transpose(list(gradients, model$trainable_variables)))
        epoch_loss_metric$update_state(loss)
        loss
      }
      
      for (epoch in 1:1) {
        print(paste('Epoch',epoch))
        self$on_epoch_begin(trial, model, epoch, logs= list())
        intializer = make_iterator_one_shot(train_ds)
        
        for (batch in 1:length(iterate(train_ds))) {
          
          init_next = iter_next(intializer)
          
          self$on_batch_begin(trial, model, batch, logs=list())
          batch_loss = run_train_step(init_next)
          self$on_batch_end(trial, model, batch, logs=list('loss' = batch_loss))
          
          if (batch %% 100L == 0L){
            loss = epoch_loss_metric$result()$numpy()
            print(paste('Batch',batch,  'Average loss', loss))
          }
        }
        
        epoch_loss = epoch_loss_metric$result()$numpy()
        self$on_epoch_end(trial, model, epoch, logs=list('loss'= epoch_loss))
        epoch_loss_metric$reset_states()
      }
    }
  )
)

oracle <- kt$oracles$BayesianOptimization(
  objective=kt$Objective('loss', 'min'),
  max_trials=2L)

tuner = MyTuner(
  oracle=oracle,
  hypermodel=conv_build_model,
  directory='results',

```
import kerastuner as kt
import tensorflow as tf
import tensorflow_datasets as tfds


def build_model(hp):
    """Builds a convolutional model."""
    inputs = tf.keras.Input(shape=(28, 28, 1))
    x = inputs
    for i in range(hp.Int('conv_layers', 1, 3, default=3)):
        x = tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(
            filters=hp.Int('filters_' + str(i), 4, 32, step=4, default=8),
            kernel_size=hp.Int('kernel_size_' + str(i), 3, 5),
            activation='relu',
            padding='same')(x)

        if hp.Choice('pooling' + str(i), ['max', 'avg']) == 'max':
            x = tf.keras.layers.MaxPooling2D()(x)
        else:
            x = tf.keras.layers.AveragePooling2D()(x)

        x = tf.keras.layers.BatchNormalization()(x)
        x = tf.keras.layers.ReLU()(x)

    if hp.Choice('global_pooling', ['max', 'avg']) == 'max':
        x = tf.keras.layers.GlobalMaxPooling2D()(x)
    else:
        x = tf.keras.layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(x)
    outputs = tf.keras.layers.Dense(10, activation='softmax')(x)

    model = tf.keras.Model(inputs, outputs)

    optimizer = hp.Choice('optimizer', ['adam', 'sgd'])
    model.compile(optimizer, loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy', metrics=['accuracy'])
    return model


class MyTuner(kt.Tuner):

    def run_trial(self, trial, train_ds):
        hp = trial.hyperparameters

        # Hyperparameters can be added anywhere inside `run_trial`.
        # When the first trial is run, they will take on their default values.
        # Afterwards, they will be tuned by the `Oracle`.
        train_ds = train_ds.batch(
            hp.Int('batch_size', 32, 128, step=32, default=64))

        model = self.hypermodel.build(trial.hyperparameters)
        lr = hp.Float('learning_rate', 1e-4, 1e-2, sampling='log', default=1e-3)
        optimizer = tf.keras.optimizers.Adam(lr)
        epoch_loss_metric = tf.keras.metrics.Mean()

        @tf.function
        def run_train_step(data):
            images = tf.dtypes.cast(data['image'], 'float32') / 255.
            labels = data['label']
            with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
                logits = model(images)
                loss = tf.keras.losses.sparse_categorical_crossentropy(
                    labels, logits)
                # Add any regularization losses.
                if model.losses:
                    loss += tf.math.add_n(model.losses)
                gradients = tape.gradient(loss, model.trainable_variables)
            optimizer.apply_gradients(zip(gradients, model.trainable_variables))
            epoch_loss_metric.update_state(loss)
            return loss

        # `self.on_epoch_end` reports results to the `Oracle` and saves the
        # current state of the Model. The other hooks called here only log values
        # for display but can also be overridden. For use cases where there is no
        # natural concept of epoch, you do not have to call any of these hooks. In
        # this case you should instead call `self.oracle.update_trial` and
        # `self.oracle.save_model` manually.
        for epoch in range(10):
            print('Epoch: {}'.format(epoch))

            self.on_epoch_begin(trial, model, epoch, logs={})
            for batch, data in enumerate(train_ds):
                self.on_batch_begin(trial, model, batch, logs={})
                batch_loss = float(run_train_step(data))
                self.on_batch_end(trial, model, batch, logs={'loss': batch_loss})

                if batch % 100 == 0:
                    loss = epoch_loss_metric.result().numpy()
                    print('Batch: {}, Average Loss: {}'.format(batch, loss))

            epoch_loss = epoch_loss_metric.result().numpy()
            self.on_epoch_end(trial, model, epoch, logs={'loss': epoch_loss})
            epoch_loss_metric.reset_states()


def main():
  tuner = MyTuner(
      oracle=kt.oracles.BayesianOptimization(
          objective=kt.Objective('loss', 'min'),
          max_trials=2),
      hypermodel=build_model,
      directory='results',
      project_name='mnist_custom_training')

  mnist_data = tfds.load('mnist')
  mnist_train, mnist_test = mnist_data['train'], mnist_data['test']
  mnist_train = mnist_train.shuffle(1000)

  tuner.search(train_ds=mnist_train)

  best_hps = tuner.get_best_hyperparameters()[0]
  print(best_hps.values)

  best_model = tuner.get_best_models()[0]

if __name__ == '__main__':
  main()
```

Below is a minimal working example that showcases, in principle, what I'm trying to achieve and highlights the issue that I'm having:

```
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```
Import reticulate and define an R object:
```
library(reticulate)
a = 5 # Variable declared in global environment
```
Define an R function:
```
printPython = function(){
  b = 2 # Variable declared within the scope of the function
  # Attempt to translate both to python and run a python command:
  py_run_string("print(r.a)")

Execute the function:

printPython()

printPythonGlobal = function() {

title: Inconsistent documentation for conda_install
description:
While the documentation specifies that `pip_ignore_installed` is `TRUE` by default, it in fact defaults to `FALSE`:

https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/3529aaff1c9e528a303d5d9c3c3ccb0f07301a83/R/conda.R#L185-L217

title: Allow conda package match specifications in python_version
description:
Having the equal sign hard-coded in `conda_install` prohibits the use of [conda package match specifications](https://docs.conda.io/projects/conda-build/en/latest/resources/package-spec.html#package-match-specifications) in the `python_version` argument (e.g. `python_version=">=3.8"`):

https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/284c24f66a7dee8da02b214ff6f1530c314b5cd4/R/conda.R#L231

I propose to only add the equal sign, if no match specification is given (but still add it in this case, to ensure backwards compatibility).

title: Timezone naive datetime.datetime objects fail because of py_to_r.datetime.datetime()
description:
Trying to construct or return a 'naive' `datetime.datetime` object (that is, one without time zone information) fails because of a bug in `py_to_r.datetime.datetime()`. The same problem arises if automatic conversions are disabled and an instance of this kind of `datetime` object is expressly converted using `py_to_r`.

MWE:
```{R}
library(reticulate)
datetime <- import("datetime")
d <- datetime$datetime(
  year = 2020L,
  month = 8L,
  day = 24L,
  tzinfo = NULL
)
```
> Error in if (tzname %in% c("UTC", "UTC+00:00")) return(as.POSIXct(posix,  : 
>   argument is of length zero

`d$tzname` in this case is `None`, `tzname` in the function becomes `NULL`, and the `if(...)` evaluates to `logical(0)`.

I have to say that I'm not quite sure what is going on in this function in general. In HEAD, the code looks like the following:
```{R}
  # preserve timezone if available (handle UTC explicitly)
  tzname <- as_r_value(x$tzname())
  if (tzname %in% c("UTC", "UTC+00:00"))
    return(as.POSIXct(posix, origin = "1970-01-01", tz = "UTC"))
  
  # treat other times as local / system times
  as.POSIXct(posix, origin = "1970-01-01", tz = "UTC")
```
As the same value is being returned irrespective of the result of the test, and neither branch seems to do what the comments suggest (the first only preserves timezone if it's UTC, the second does not treat as a local time but imposes UTC anyway) I have not attempted a patch: I think someone with a deeper understanding of how to handle dates in R and python should take a look and decide what behaviour is actually wanted.

title: Matplotlib backend failure crashes headless sessions, even if no Matplotlib used
description:
I finally tracked down a crash that we were facing inconsistently with reticulate on an RStudio Server instance.

Knitting would work fine, running the code in `repl_python()` would work fine, but running code chunks within RStudio would crash, with nothing in the server logs other than the useless "hadabend".

Finally I happened to see a message flash by about failing to connect to display, right before the session crashed. So my mitigation is to insert, before the first Python chunk:

```r
py_run_string("import matplotlib.pyplot as plt; plt.switch_backend('agg')")
```

This, despite the crashing Rmd *not doing anything graphical or matplotlib-related whatsoever*.

(Oddly, importing matplotlib in `repl_python` in the console would work just fine even without this, and reported 'agg' as the backend.)

Clearly I haven't located the *root* cause of this error yet, but now we can at least have a reasonable theory about what's going on.

Related: https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/issues/470

It appears the scope of a variable named `r` does not persist across Python chunks. For example:

````
```{python}
r = 0
print(r)
```
````

Prints `0` as expected. But then the immediately following chunk:

````
```{python}
print(r)
```
````

Prints `<__main__.R object at 0x000001F1458F4B08>` instead.

Switching the variable name to something else, like `s`, works as expected though, i.e. prints `0` in both chunks above. Would be great to have similar behavior for variables named `r` too. Thanks.

title: Simplify importing of multiindex DataFrames into R
description:
One problem I often encounter is to wanting to import a pandas ```DataFrame``` with a multiindex into R.

As far as I can see reticulate can import it, but puts the index into an attribute. I can see the value in that, but more useful for scenarios where you would never go back to python would be to get the index as columns in the ```data.frame``` instead, i.e. like by ```reset_index()``` in pandas. Since the ```DataFrame``` has already been converted I guess it would be too late to call ```reset_index()``` on it.

Is there currently a way of resetting a multiindex after converting to R?

If not, I might, given some pointers, be able to work on getting such functionality into reticulate.

Two options would be:

* Have a function in reticulate to do ```reset_index()``` using the index in the attribute
* Have a global option in reticulate to automatically always reset multiindices.

`class Dim_TruncatedSVD(Unit):
    def __init__(self, n_components='knee', n_components_max=30, **kwargs):
        self.n_components = n_components
        self.n_components_max = n_components_max
        self.kwargs = kwargs
    def get(self, x, return_evr=False):
        if self.n_components == 'knee':
            n_components = min(self.n_components_max, np.min(x.shape))
            obj = TruncatedSVD(n_components=n_components, **self.kwargs).fit(x)

            # Construct axis for KneeLocator
            x_axis = list(range(1, n_components + 1))
            y_axis = obj.explained_variance_ratio_
            # Find knee
            n_components = KneeLocator(x_axis, y_axis,

            n_components = max(n_components, 10)
            x_emb = TruncatedSVD(n_components=n_components,

        else:
            x_emb = TruncatedSVD(n_components=self.n_components,
                                 **self.kwargs).fit_transform(x)
        if return_evr == True:
            return x_emb, y_axis
        else:

I have the same setup in Ubuntu 16.04 and python3.8.5 and python3.7.8 installed locally but reticulate is able to detect libpython from the python binaries (can't check the detailed configuration and versions there since I have no access to that machine at the moment)

description:
I have a .Rmd file containing the following two chunks:

`````
```{r}
x = data.frame(甲=1:3, 乙=4:6)

```{python}
r.x
```
`````

> Error in py_call_impl(callable, dots$args, dots$keywords) :

I have tried to present some reproducible examples of what works and what doesn't, please see below.

Sys.which("python")

title: Checking Python package version triggering winbuilder NOTE on R-devel
description:
In an R package we added a function for checking if the version of the wrapped Python package is sufficiently up-to-date.

https://github.com/ropensci/rdataretriever/blob/486bcf3a14be79ea398b93ffb99474e38de94adc/R/rdataretriever.R#L173-L196

This function is called in `.onLoad`, wrapped inside the recommended `try` block after `reticulate::import`:

https://github.com/ropensci/rdataretriever/blob/486bcf3a14be79ea398b93ffb99474e38de94adc/R/rdataretriever.R#L768-L774

This tests fine locally using `R CMD check` with `--as-cran` and passes on winbuilder, except for Windows on R-devel, which returns a NOTE:

```
Warning in system2(command = python, args = paste0("\"", config_script,  :
  running command '"C:/Users/ligges/AppData/Local/r-miniconda/envs/r-reticulate/python.exe" "d:/RCompile/CRANpkg/lib/4.1/reticulate/config/config.py"' had status 2

A namespace must be able to be loaded with just the base namespace
loaded: otherwise if the namespace gets loaded by a saved object, the
session will be unable to start.

Probably some imports need to be declared in the NAMESPACE file.
```

Link to winbuilder output: https://win-builder.r-project.org/incoming_pretest/rdataretriever_3.0.0_20200804_163723/Windows/00check.log

Any advice for avoiding this note or direction to guidance on better practice for performing version checks of associated Python packages would be greatly appreciated.

Linking to the issue in our repo: https://github.com/ropensci/rdataretriever/issues/242

title: install python packages in renv-enabled project
description:
I'm in a renv-enabled project and used `renv::use_python(type = "conda")`.

Sorry for no reprex.. it's a little hard to do it with `renv`. 

I think that `conda_binary()` isn't working properly with a minimal conda env created by `renv::use_python()`, which causes python packages fail to install.  

In the project, when I try to install a python packages with `py_install()`:

```
> py_install("numpy") 
sh: /path/to/project/renv/python/condaenvs/renv-python: Is a directory Error: installation of 'python' into environment '/path/to/project/renv/python/condaenvs/renv-python' failed [error code 126]
```

Tracking the error, I found that `reticulate::py_install()` calls `reticulate::conda_binary()` to find conda binary, with the input being the renv-created conda env path (in this case, `/path/to/project/renv/python/condaenvs/renv-python`). Instead of locating the conda binary within this env at `/path/to/project/renv/python/condaenvs/renv-python/bin/conda`, it just returns the orignal path back. 

When I do this, it worked:

```
py_install("numpy", envname = "renv/python/condaenvs/renv-python")
```

this also works:

```
conda_install(packages = "numpy")
```

I _think_ the problem comes from this logic here for renv-created conda envs:

https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/master/R/install.R#L89-L99
