title: FR: allow user to force pure conda tensorflow install
description:
NOTE: moving issue from rstudio/tensorflow at request of @jjallaire [here](https://github.com/rstudio/tensorflow/issues/281#issuecomment-444889825)

---------------------

Thanks so much for all your work on reticulate, tensorflow, and keras - truly fantastic!

I'm working on a shared computing platform running CentOS 7, and `install_tensorflow()` was failing. After some tinkering in conda I believe it is because `pip` is not functional in our platform even when it's running from within a conda environment.

I was able to successfully execute `install_tensorflow()` by using `debug()` and:

1. Changing `packages` to "tensorflow" after [this line](https://github.com/rstudio/tensorflow/blob/14beca91750604b1a586f33bb895bbe81b9a3840/R/install.R#L328) sets it based on googleapis.com
2. Stepping into [this call to `conda_install()`](https://github.com/rstudio/tensorflow/blob/14beca91750604b1a586f33bb895bbe81b9a3840/R/install.R#L346) and setting `pip = FALSE`
3. Stepping into [this call to `conda_install()`](https://github.com/rstudio/tensorflow/blob/14beca91750604b1a586f33bb895bbe81b9a3840/R/install.R#L356) and setting `pip = FALSE`

Even though `pip` is the officially supported way to install tensorflow and keras, would it be possible to add an argument to `install_tensorflow()` that forces a pure conda install (as in the [windows short-circuit](https://github.com/rstudio/tensorflow/blob/14beca91750604b1a586f33bb895bbe81b9a3840/R/install.R#L285)) for people in situations like mine?

It could print a note that GPU installs are not available via conda and that `pip` is the only officially supported installation method so people understand they're going rogue.

Alternatively, the documentation could inform users that they can and demonstrate how to create and configure the `r-tensorflow` conda environment in conda then run a tensorflow version of `is_keras_available()` to confirm R can successfully access and use the environment.

Thanks for considering!

EDIT: pip specification of `--user` as described [here](https://github.com/rstudio/tensorflow/issues/246#issuecomment-415799413) might be relevant to why it wasn't working for me, but I'm neither sysadmin nor python savvy so not sure.

EDIT 2: I now see the instructions in the [tensorflow custom installation section](https://tensorflow.rstudio.com/tensorflow/articles/installation.html#custom-installation) for how to point `keras` to an appropriate conda environment one has created outside of R, which I had not noticed when I wrote the original FR.

title: weird issue with dynamic imports?
description:
Hello the `reticulate` team. I am escalating this issue with you because I was unable to solve it otherwise.

Please see here https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/issues/2982

Here is the issue: I am perfectly able to use the well-known Spacy package in python and, in particular, to  load my custom model in `spyder`

```
Python 3.6.6 |Anaconda custom (64-bit)| (default, Jun 28 2018, 17:14:51)
Type "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.

IPython 6.5.0 -- An enhanced Interactive Python.

import spacy

nlp = spacy.load('/otherdrive/model/en_core_web_lg-2.0.0/en_core_web_lg/en_core_web_lg-2.0.0')

```

Now doing the same exact thing in R (using `reticulate`) triggers an error when `spacy` apparently cannot load the `en` model (even though I pointed toward a specific folder)
```

library(reticulate)
use_python("/mydrive/anaconda/bin/python")

py_run_string("import spacy")
py_run_string("nlp = spacy.load('/otherdrive/model/en_core_web_lg-2.0.0/en_core_web_lg/en_core_web_lg-2.0.0')")
 ImportError: [E048] Can't import language en from spacy.lang.
```

After discussin a bit with @ines ,
> Thanks for the report! There's not really an "`en` model" – that's just the shortcut for the `en_core_web_sm` package. What the error means here is that it can't load the `spacy.lang.en` module containing the language data to initialize the language class.
> 
> Because some languages now ship with a lot of language data, spaCy lazy-loads the modules only when needed – see here for how this is implemented (including when the erorr is raised):
> 
> [spaCy/spacy/util.py](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/658f7e0dc8f79132f74bc52d2c3e92fc62fc454f/spacy/util.py#L41-L54)
> 
> Lines 41 to 54 in [658f7e0](/explosion/spaCy/commit/658f7e0dc8f79132f74bc52d2c3e92fc62fc454f)
> 
>  def get_lang_class(lang): 
>      """Import and load a Language class. 
>   
>      lang (unicode): Two-letter language code, e.g. 'en'. 
>      RETURNS (Language): Language class. 
>      """ 
>      global LANGUAGES 
>      if lang not in LANGUAGES: 
>          try: 
>              module = importlib.import_module('.lang.%s' % lang, 'spacy') 
>          except ImportError: 
>              raise ImportError(Errors.E048.format(lang=lang)) 
>          LANGUAGES[lang] = getattr(module, module.__all__[0]) 
>      return LANGUAGES[lang] 
> Is it possible that reticulate somehow handles the dynamic imports differently? One thing you could try is edit that file in your spaCy installation, remove the `try`/`except` block and have a look at the original error and traceback. Maybe this gives us better insight into why it fails to import the module?

What do you think?
THanks!!

getter <- function(self, code) {

        if ( is.function(r_variable) ) {

title: session cannot be stopped in Rstudio while using pyfmi do co-simulation
description:
Thanks for the fantastic package!

I wanna use the pyFMI python module which is aimed at loading and interacting with Functional Mock-Up Units(FMUs) for co-simulation between R(python) and Energyplus(A building simulation program). But the Rstudio session cannot be stopped while running the following codes:

```
rm(list = ls())
library(reticulate)

use_python('F:/ProgramData/Anaconda3')
pyfmi <- import('pyfmi')

model <- pyfmi$load_fmu('path to FMU file.fmu')

t_start <- 60 * 60 * 24 * 180
t_end <- 60 * 60 * 24 * 200
t_step_size <- 15 * 60

model$instantiate_slave()
model$initialize(t_start, t_end, TRUE)
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/33275527/48463458-07f21e80-e817-11e8-9acd-3fb689bd7f02.png)

The final line `model$initialize(t_start,t_end,TRUE)`will call the CMD( in windows OS) to initialize the FMU(also call EnergyPlus software). The CMD windows will not be closed and wait the further code to control the Energyplus simulation.Therefore, I guess Rstudio cannot judge the CMD status rightly, thus causing the final line never stop.

The codes work successfully in R but not Rstudio. Meanwhile, I use the Jobs background in the preview release of Rstudio to run this code, it also works. 

In R, it works:

![r](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/33275527/48467043-b8195480-e822-11e8-8278-a35e4687e60f.gif)

It also works in Jobs of Rstudio preview release

![rstudio 2](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/33275527/48467442-dcc1fc00-e823-11e8-859a-d787977d2346.gif)

I guess there are problems between the interacting of Rstudio console and CMD, thus causing Rstudio cannot judge the CMD status rightly and think the initialize codes is running abidingly.


Is there any way to run the code in Rstudio successfully? Any suggestions are pleasure!

Thanks!
JY

title: Cannot import rdkit module
description:
I am having trouble importing a specific module using reticulate within R (Feather Spray, version 3.5.1) and RStudio (version 1.1.456) on my MacBook Pro running High Sierra.  The Python module I'm working with is called RDKit (https://github.com/rdkit/rdkit).  The package works fine on the same computer when importing from the Python command line (or Spyder for that matter):
```
>>> import rdkit
import rdkit # directory /Users/pleeferguson/apps/rdkit/rdkit
# /Users/pleeferguson/apps/rdkit/rdkit/__init__.pyc matches /Users/pleeferguson/apps/rdkit/rdkit/__init__.py
import rdkit # precompiled from /Users/pleeferguson/apps/rdkit/rdkit/__init__.pyc
dlopen("/Users/pleeferguson/apps/rdkit/rdkit/rdBase.so", 2);
import rdkit.rdBase # dynamically loaded from /Users/pleeferguson/apps/rdkit/rdkit/rdBase.so
>>>
```
When I try to import RDKit within RStudio using reticulate, it fails as follows:
```
> reticulate::use_python("/Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/2.7/bin/python")
> library(reticulate)
> rdkit <- import_from_path("rdkit", "/Users/pleeferguson/apps/rdkit/rdkit")
Error in py_module_import(module, convert = convert) : 
  ImportError: No module named rdBase
> 
```
I also tried to import the module directly within R from the terminal (outside of RStudio), where I got a little more informative error message:
```
> reticulate::use_python("/Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/2.7/bin/python")
> library(reticulate)
> rdkit <- import("rdkit")
Error in py_module_import(module, convert = convert) : 
  ImportError: dlopen(/Users/pleeferguson/apps/rdkit/rdkit/rdBase.so, 2): Library not loaded: @rpath/libRDKitRDBoost.1.dylib
  Referenced from: /Users/pleeferguson/apps/rdkit/rdkit/rdBase.so
  Reason: image not found

Detailed traceback: 
  File "/Users/pleeferguson/apps/rdkit/rdkit/__init__.py", line 2, in <module>
    from .rdBase import rdkitVersion as __version__
>
```
I've verified that there is indeed a symlink named `libRDKitRDBoost.1.dylib` at the right place and pointing to the correct dylib file (it does exist within the lib directory of the RDKit package).

Also, I have no trouble importing other packages (e.g. pandas) within RStudio using reticulate:
```
> reticulate::use_python("/Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/2.7/bin/python")
> library(reticulate)
> pd <- import("pandas", as = "pd")
> 
```
On my other MacBook Pro with an earlier version of both R (Sincere Pumpkin Patch) and RDKit (2015 build), the rdkit package loads just fine (and is functional) from within RStudio, using reticulate.

Any ideas what might be happening here?  I don't think it is an RStudio issue, as I've tried installing the newest daily build of RStudio but get the same behavior.  Also, the fact that I can't get the package to import from R within the terminal (outside of RStudio) tells me it must be something else.

title: Please allow blind R users to access the `py_help()` output
description:
Hello,

I am a blind person using a screen reading program when doing R.
The current output type of `reticulate::py_help()` is not accessible for assistive technologies like screen reader software.
As an alternative, the HTML output format can be made accessible.
Please consider either adding the following function to `reticulate` package or allowing users to specify help output format as an argument for `reticulate::py_help()` function.

``` r
# The function below is retrieved from https://www.r-bloggers.com/digging-into-mbox-details-a-tale-of-tm-reticulate/

py_doc <- function(x) {
  require("htmltools")
  require("reticulate")
  pydoc <- reticulate::import("pydoc")
  htmltools::html_print(
    htmltools::HTML(
      pydoc$render_doc(x, renderer=pydoc$HTMLDoc())

  )
}

title: python lists with None
description:
Here is a function that will return a list containing None

```
def bad_function():
    return ["hello", None]
```

I was hoping reticulate would convert this to a character vector containing a NA. Unfortunately it returns back a list, which I then have to reconstruct into a vector

```
require(reticulate)
source_python("bad_function.py")
bad_function()

[[1]]
[1] "hello"

[[2]]
NULL
```

I think this happens because https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/7869d13544ecc13284a8a3f12025643e80c1e6a1/src/python.cpp#L570 will return NILSXP, which means inside `py_to_r` it will not create a Rcpp CharacterVector. One possible way to work around this might be to check for `None` before `if (r_scalar_type(next) != scalarType)`

title: python longs in data.frame
description:
I have a python function which returns longs in python. R integers can only go to about 10^9, so translating python long to R integer can cause an overflow.

I think the overflow comes from these lines, where a long is converted to a INTSXP

https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/7869d13544ecc13284a8a3f12025643e80c1e6a1/src/python.cpp#L536

Is there a way for reticulate to map python longs to R numerics? or integer.64?

title: Request for parallelized pandas -> data frame conversion

title: Issue warning if repl_python() can't find the executable set by use_python()
description:
If `use_python()` was invoked using an invalid path, `repl_python()` uses whatever python executable it can find instead.

Suggestion: issue a warning stating that the path set by `use_python()` was not found and that `repl_python()` is falling back on what it can find. The executable being used is already identified at the start, but the warning will explain why the "wrong" python is being used.

-----

In this examples, `python42` is not a valid path, but `/usr/bin/python3` is.
```
Restarting R session...

> library(reticulate)
> use_python("python42")
> reticulate::repl_python()
Python 2.7.12 (/usr/bin/python)
Reticulate 1.10 REPL -- A Python interpreter in R.
>>> import sys
>>> print(sys.executable)
/usr/bin/python
>>> quit

Restarting R session...

> library(reticulate)

Python 2.7.12 (/usr/bin/python)
Reticulate 1.10 REPL -- A Python interpreter in R.
>>> import sys

/usr/bin/python
>>> quit

Restarting R session...

> library(reticulate)

Python 3.5.2 (/usr/bin/python3)
Reticulate 1.10 REPL -- A Python interpreter in R.

/usr/bin/python3
>>> quit
```

**Issue**: When using pandas backfill function, the output is correct in a python notebook, but gives an incorrect result when the same code is called from R using the Reticulate package.

**Context**: I am trying to use a backfill function to do a last observation carried backwards. I used tidyr's fill function with .direction = "up" which works, but for my dataset it was taking more than an hour.

**Sample Data**: Minimal sample data is located [here](https://github.com/engti/mediadata_prep/blob/master/test1.csv).

**Jupyter Notebook Code**
So I used the following code in Python, which takes in the file, groups it by the user_id and then sorts by date and hour before applying the backfill function on the sale_index column:

```
import pandas
def read_backfill(file):
  filltest = pandas.read_csv(file)
  filltest = filltest.sort_values(['user_id', 'date', 'hour']).reset_index()
  filltest.sale_index = filltest.groupby(['user_id']).sale_index.bfill()
  return filltest
```
I called the above code with the following:
```
df1 = read_backfill('test1.csv')
df1.loc[df1['user_id']=="zxyu"]
```
Which gave me the correct output in 5 mins, which is awesome. Image of output [here](https://i.redd.it/nwcbdjzfxzh11.png).

**R Integration** 
So far so good, but I am trying to integrate this into a single workflow within R as the plotting and the markdown creation is happening here. I used the Reticulate package to call the same function which was saved as backfill.py. But here there's an issue, it just didn't give me the correct output, unlike when I called it from iPython.

## py test using the python code from above example

It would give me the following output - [image](https://i.redd.it/11azs570yzh11.png)

Any idea what's going on? It's the same code, line for line. For some reason it seems to ignore the grouping and sorting, and perform the back fill incorrectly according to some logic I don't understand.

title: Feature request: Support pip3 and PYTHONUSERBASE
description:
I'm looking to use reticulate with our students this year. To make this a bit easier I'm working on a docker container with Ubuntu 18.04, rstudio, python3, and pip3. Most of the python packages needed are already in the docker container but in case users do want to install additional packages it would be great if they could install them to a custom directory on the host system that will persist if the container is shutdown (e.g., ~/.special_dir_for_docker). title: flush stdout / stderr after py_run_string with Python 3
description:
E.g.

```R
reticulate::use_python("/usr/local/bin/python3", required = TRUE)
reticulate::py_run_string("print('hello')")
```

No output is emitted in Python 3 until the stdout / stderr streams are explicitly flushed; we should do that ourselves at the conclusion of `py_run_string()` / `py_run_file()`.

title: reticulate output in R chunks not captured in R Markdown
description:
To reproduce, try rendering the following document (repro'ed with macOS 10.13.6 + R 3.5.1):

`````
---
title: "Reticulate"
output: md_document
---
  
```{r}
reticulate::py_run_string("print('hello')")
```
`````

You'll see that the printed output (`hello`) is not captured and reflected in the generated Markdown document.

I think the issue here is that `knitr` attempts to capture R output with a `sink()`; however, because we don't always install redirects for Python output back to R, that output is lost. See e.g.:

https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/82b2eb822469f3cd0dc0fe2ca34d55c65b998474/R/output.R#L3-L11

The fix here would likely be to ensure that the output streams are remapped when we're running `reticulate` within `knitr` -- or perhaps we should just always unconditionally remap the output streams.

See also: https://github.com/rstudio/rstudio/issues/3271

title: Suggestion : support running Sagemath as a python engine.
description:
[Sagemath](http://www.sagemath.org/) (a. k. a. Sage) is a mathematics software written in (and close to) Python. Its interactive environment is IPython, and it accepts *grosso modo* almost any legan python code (Python 2 at the moment, but support for Python3 is coming). Its REPL preprocesses inputs (for example, 2^3 is interpreted as 2**3). Of course, it extends python a lot in the math department.

Having `reticulate` support it would make R users able to use Sage symbolic and algebraic abilities. For example, a paper written with `knitr` or `Rmarkdown` could also use Sage for symbolic calculations supporting the R code.

Something like this can currently be (awkwardly) done by using both `knitr` and either [Sagetex](https://github.com/sagemath/sagetex) or [Pythontex](https://github.com/gpoore/pythontex) from a .Rnw file.  Using this is a bit involved. it implies : 
* `knit` the `.rnw` file to `.tex`
* `\LaTeX` the `.tex` file at least once
* `sage` or `pythontex the relevant files
* re-`LaTeX` the `.tex` file at least once.

Doing this from `.Rmd` file is even more awkward : the relevant Sage chunks can be wrapped in \LaTeX-only chunks (you end the chunk with `{=latex}`), and you have to manually run Sage or Pythontex and \Latex again...

With a Sage-enabled `reticulate`, the normal mechanisms for knitting should suffice. Much simpler...

(The only alternative I am aware of is to use `sympy` from Python. This can be done already, but entails losing a lot of Sage-specific abilities (as well as those all the subsystems Sage can use, such as Maxima, Pari, Singular (and sympy itself), or even Maple, Mathematica or Fricas).

I checked that running reticulate by passing it the location of the shell script that starts Sage is not enough : one gets an interaction with the Python interpreter supporting Sage : 
```
> library(reticulate)
> use_python("/usr/local/sage-8/sage")
> repl_python()
Python 2.7.15 (/usr/local/sage-8/sage)
Reticulate 1.9 REPL -- A Python interpreter in R.
>>> 2+3
5
```
The Python interpreter seems to work. But this is not enough to get Sage working : 
```
>>> from sage.all import *
TypeError: sequence item 0: expected string, NoneType found
>>> 2^3
1
```
We are still in Python, no preprocessing
```
>>> sage.var("x")
NameError: name 'sage' is not defined
``` 
and the import *really* failed
```
>>> exit
> 
```
At least, this didn't seem to cause trouble on R's side...

Thoughts ?

title: r_to_py()/py_to_r() timezones
description:
Could `r_to_py()` and `py_to_r()` be adapted for cases where the source data has columns with timezone attributes, such that the timezone is set in the target data?

Could this be done without stepping on \#160? (tagging @DavisVaughan) On this question, I wonder if a distinction can be made between tz-naive `datetime64[ns]` and tz-aware `datetime64[ns, <tz>]`.

-----

My experience with Python is limited, so maybe the best thing I can do is to demonstrate. In my Rmd, I am using both R and Python chunks, so I will label those explicitly to appear in the Markdown.

``` r
# R
library("reticulate")
library("readr")
# imports "glue"

pd <- import("pandas")

# function to describe the attributes of a POSIXct:
describe <- function(x) {
  
  as_utc <- x
  attr(as_utc, "tzone") <- "UTC"
  
  str_value <- formatC(as.numeric(x) * 1000, digits = 13, width = 13)
  
  print(
    glue::glue("UTC time:       {as_utc}"),
    glue::glue("Formatted time: {x}"),
    glue::glue("Timezone:       {attr(x, 'tzone')}"),
    glue::glue("Milliseconds:   {str_value}")
  )
  
  invisible(x)
}
```

``` python
# Python
import pandas as pd

# function to describe the attributes of the datetime64
def describe(x):
    if x.tzinfo is None:
      utc_time = 'not defined'
    else:
      utc_time = x.tz_convert('UTC')
    
    print('UTC time:       ', utc_time)
    print('Formatted time: ', x)
    print('Timezone:       ', x.tzinfo)
    print('Milliseconds:   ', x.value / 1.e6)
    print('')
    print(pd.DataFrame({'x' : [x]}).dtypes)
    return x
```

-----

For the first step, let’s create a data frame in R that we will send to Python. It will have a single column with a single value.

``` r
# R
df_r_to_py <- 
  data.frame(
    x = parse_datetime(
      "2013-04-05T06:00:00Z", 
      locale = locale(tz = "America/Chicago")
    )
  )

describe(df_r_to_py$x)
```

    ## UTC time:       2013-04-05 06:00:00
    ## Formatted time: 2013-04-05 01:00:00
    ## Timezone:       America/Chicago
    ## Milliseconds:   1365141600000

So far, so good.

-----

Let’s see what Python sees:

``` python
# Python
describe(r.df_r_to_py.x[0])
```

    ## UTC time:        not defined
    ## Formatted time:  2013-04-05 06:00:00
    ## Timezone:        None
    ## Milliseconds:    1365141600000.0
    ## 
    ## x    datetime64[ns]
    ## dtype: object

We see that the numerical representation has been “preserved”, but that the localization has not been brought over.

-----

In Python, let’s create a copy of what was sent from R, then let’s do the localization manually.

``` python
# Python
df_py_to_r = r.df_r_to_py.copy()
df_py_to_r.x = df_py_to_r.x.dt.tz_localize('UTC').dt.tz_convert('America/Chicago')
describe(df_py_to_r.x[0])
```

    ## UTC time:        2013-04-05 06:00:00+00:00
    ## Formatted time:  2013-04-05 01:00:00-05:00
    ## Timezone:        America/Chicago
    ## Milliseconds:    1365141600000.0
    ## 
    ## x    datetime64[ns, America/Chicago]
    ## dtype: object

This looks good now.

-----

Finally, let’s look at this in R:

``` r
# R
df_return <- py$df_py_to_r

describe(df_return$x)
```

    ## UTC time:       2013-04-05 06:00:00
    ## Formatted time: 2013-04-05 06:00:00
    ## Timezone:       UTC
    ## Milliseconds:   1365141600000

Here, there seems to be partially good-news. The numerical value has been preserved, and the timezone is set.

The “bad” news is that the timezone is set to `"UTC"`, but this is one of the behaviors sought in \#160 (but perhaps only for the tz-naive case).

## Summary

Just to restate from the top:

Could `r_to_py()` and `py_to_r()` be adapted for cases where the source data has columns with timezone attributes, such that the timezone is set in the target data?

Could this be done without stepping on \#160? On this question, I wonder if a distinction can be made between tz-naive `datetime64[ns]` and tz-aware `datetime64[ns, <tz>]`.

title: Incompatibility with reticulate and rpy2
description:
I have a code base that is in python and I am trying to integrate an R library into it. I am using `rpy2` to call an R function. 

I've found that if the R function calls reticulate, it will cause a segfault (core dumped). I think this is because of the circular nature of using Python to call R to call Python. However, I felt this use case might be common: for example an R developer might write a function `foo` that uses `sparse.model.matrix`, and passes that data to scipy through reticulate. A python developer that is trying to integrate the library into the application `bar` wants to call `foo` directly - this will cause the segfault. The developers could coordinate so that `foo` only returns the sparse matrix without calling scipy, and the application `bar` receives the sparse matrix and calls scipy itself. This is pretty challenging, so I'm wondering if there is something simpler I am missing to handle this edge case.

Here is a reproducible example of python calling R calling python.

```
from rpy2.robjects.packages import importr
import rpy2.robjects as robjects

r_func = robjects.r('''
  myfunc = function() {
    require(reticulate)
    sys = import("sys")
  }
  ''')
  
response = r_func()
```

```

title: py_to_r() fails when when importing a python module with an alias
description:
I am using the reticulate package to integrate Python into an R package I'm building (hitfuture/Neo4jDriveR). One of the capabilities I need is to return R data.frames from a method in the R6 based object model. I utilize Python Pandas package to create a DataFrame in the reticulate Python environment. My objective is to return an R data.frame. The issue I'm seeing is that when I used reticulate::py_to_r(df) it does not convert to R and instead it returns a python DataFrame object. The problem is based on the way reticulate::import() is utilized.

I had forked reticulate into my github repository so I am using the latest version (1.9.0.9001). I see that there are well defined S3 methods to handle pandas DataFrame conversion in the reticulate py_to_r() S3 class (e.g. py_to_r.pandas.core.frame.DataFrame).   The following test executes correctly in a new R session.

py_config()
```

```

print(class(convert))
```

```
## [1] "pandas.core.frame.DataFrame"

The failure occurs when I utilize the function 'reticulate::import("pandas", as="pd")' with the `as` parameter.   You can see below that the pandas.DataFrame is not converted into an R data.frame.  The problem is due to the S3 method for the pandas DataFrame not matching based on the name of the python module.

py_config()
```

## 
## NOTE: Python version was forced by RETICULATE_PYTHON
```

```r
before <- iris 
expect_is(before,class = "data.frame")

convert <- r_to_py(before)
expect_is(convert,class = "pd.core.frame.DataFrame")

after  <- py_to_r(convert)
print(class(after))
```

```
## [1] "pd.core.frame.DataFrame"        "pd.core.generic.NDFrame"       
## [3] "pd.core.base.PandasObject"      "pd.core.base.StringMixin"

This will apply to all py_to_r conversions if the alias is not equivalent to the default name.  There is not an easy solution to solve this with the S3 methodology.  It would be good if the S3 methods are exported in the reticulate package so this can be handled manually. This should also be documented.

Thanks,
Brett

title: argument autocompletion fails for built-in functions
description:
For example:

```r
library(reticulate)
np <- import("numpy")
np$arange(<TAB>)
```

No completion items are returned. More specifically, this fails to return arguments:

```r
reticulate:::help_formals_handler.python.builtin.object("arange", np)
```

This may ultimately be a limitation of Python. From https://docs.python.org/3.8/library/inspect.html:

> Note Some callables may not be introspectable in certain implementations of Python. For example, in CPython, some built-in functions defined in C provide no metadata about their arguments.

For NumPy functions implemented in native code, we could fall back to parsing the parameter documentation for getting the available arguments.

title: Converting R raw vector to python
description:
I am trying to serialize some complex R objects to python.  I want to serialize the R object, and pass the raw bytes over. I've found some odd behavior when using RawVectors with reticulate.

In R I can generate raw using

`writeBin('hello', raw())`

Python can understand raw, for example

`"68656c6c6f00".decode("hex")`

This correctly decodes the raw to 'hello'. I can seamlessly pass these raw bytes around, for example

`writeBin('hello', raw()) %>% r_to_py %>% py_to_r`

For more complex R objects I want to use `serialize`, because writeBin can only operate on vectors. For example

`serialize(list("hello", 1:3), NULL) %>% r_to_py() %>% py_to_r`

However, the python side picks this up as just "X\n". What could be going on here?

***

Following up, I've found that the "X\n" is a header that is attached whenever serialize is called. This header is not generated for writeBin. It also contains some null bytes
```
> serialize(list('hello', 1:3), NULL) %>% rawToChar
Error in rawToChar(.) : 
  embedded nul in string: 'X\n\0\0\0\002\0\003\004\004\0\002\003\0\0\0\0\023\0\0\0\002\0\0\0\020\0\0\0\001\0\004\0\t\0\0\0\005hello\0\0\0\r\0\0\0\003\0\0\0\001\0\0\0\002\0\0\0\003'
```

It seems that python stops reading the bytes after the \0, hence it only sends back "X\n". The r_to_py method for Raw types is mainly implemented [here](https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/91ba73dd457ce111cb58631893d7b148e1a3b328/src/python.cpp#L157)

title: Interpreter used for new Virtual Environment
description:
Hi!

Firstly, I'm loving working with `reticulate`! I'm using the version of `reticulate` from GitHub (1.8.0.9000).

I am, however, having some trouble creating virtual environments which use Python 3.

For example:

```
> virtualenv_create("test")
Creating virtualenv at  /home/colliera/.virtualenv/test 
New python executable in /home/colliera/.virtualenv/test/bin/python
Installing setuptools, pip, wheel...done.
```

The new virtual environment is created with the Python 2 interpreter (although I have Python 3 on my system and reticulate is actually running with Python 3 too).

```
> py_config()
python:         /usr/bin/python3
libpython:      /usr/lib/python3.6/config-3.6m-x86_64-linux-gnu/libpython3.6.so
pythonhome:     /usr:/usr
version:        3.6.5 (default, Apr  1 2018, 05:46:30)  [GCC 7.3.0]
numpy:          /home/colliera/.local/lib/python3.6/site-packages/numpy
numpy_version:  1.14.5

python versions found: 
 /usr/bin/python
 /usr/bin/python3
```

I can see why this is happening:

```
> reticulate:::virtualenv_config()
$python
[1] "/usr/bin/python"

$virtualenv
[1] "/usr/local/bin/virtualenv"

$pip_version
[1] "pip"

$root
[1] "/home/colliera/.virtualenv"
```

So the virtual environment configuration is set up to use Python 2. Digging into the code for `virtualenv_config()` I see that it will always pick `python_unix_binary("python")` in preference to `python_unix_binary("python")`.

Would it not make more sense to provide a way to specify which executable should be used for the virtual environment? Or, maybe, default to the version that is being used already by `reticulate`?

I'd be very happy to submit a pull request, but before I do that I just wanted to understand whether there's reasoning behind the present implementation.

Thanks,
Andrew.

title: Metadata loss with Pandas Series
description:
Pandas Series can contain valuable metadata like an Index and a Name. Currently all of this is lost because of the use of `py_to_r(x$values)` in the conversion. (Note that Indices are required and Names are optional for Series)

``` r
library(reticulate)

pd <- import("pandas", convert = FALSE)
np <- import("numpy", convert = FALSE)

s = pd$Series(np$random$randn(5L), index=list('a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e'))
s$name = "hi"

s
#> a    0.205348
#> b    1.159546
#> c    0.720544
#> d    0.618997
#> e    0.325620
#> Name: hi, dtype: float64

py_to_r(s)
#> [1] 0.2053485 1.1595464 0.7205440 0.6189972 0.3256199
```

If you wanted to keep this information, I see 2 options. 

__1) Treat a Series as a 1 column data frame.__

- You have to explicitly catch unnamed Series, but you get the benefit of keeping that metadata if it was there.
- You implicitly get the benefit of the data frame index conversion that is in place over there.

```r
py_to_r.pandas.core.series.Series <- function(x) {
  
  disable_conversion_scope(x)

  x_name <- py_to_r(x$name)

  if(is.null(x_name)) {
    x$name <- "value"
  }

  py_to_r(x$to_frame())

}
```

Resulting in:

```r
> py_to_r.pandas.core.series.Series(s)
          hi
a -0.2501778
b  1.3094112
c  0.3495218
d  1.7427713
e -0.3065464
```

__2) Treat the Series like a named vector__

- There will be no way to keep the name (unless stored as an attribute)
- If conceptually the R equivalent of a Series is a vector this makes more sense.
- You'll have to extract out the index conversion code from `py_to_r.pandas.core.frame.DataFrame` into it's own function for use here, but it should "just work" for Series too.

```r
py_to_r.pandas.core.series.Series <- function(x) {
 
  disable_conversion_scope(x)
  x_r <- py_to_r(x$values)
  index <- x$index

  # New function
  x_r <- add_index_rownames(x_r, index)

  x_r
}
```

Resulting in:

```r
> py_to_r.pandas.core.series.Series(s)
         a          b          c          d          e 
-0.2501778  1.3094112  0.3495218  1.7427713 -0.3065464 
attr(,"pandas.index")
Index([u'a', u'b', u'c', u'd', u'e'], dtype='object')
```

title: py_load_object can't read DataFrames with duplicates in index
description:
As `py_load_object` tries to insert the Pandas DataFrame's index as `row.names` in the R `data.frame`, it will fail whenever the index contains duplicate values (which is allowed in a Pandas DataFrame).

Here's a sample Python code to create a pickle file with a duplicate value in the index:
```
d = {'one' : [1., 2., 3., 4.],
     'two' : [4., 3., 2., 1.]}
df = pd.DataFrame(d, index=['a', 'a', 'c', 'd'])
pickle.dump(df, open("test.pkl", "wb"))
```
And then this R code will fail:
```
library(reticulate)
pandas <- import("pandas")
df <- py_load_object("test.pkl", pickle = "pickle")
```
The exact error message:

title: Support for (python) plotly figures
description:

```python

       'layout':go.Layout(title='Plot generated in python')}
plotly.offline.iplot(fig)

## {'application/vnd.plotly.v1+json': {'data': [{'type': 'scatter', 'x': [1, 2, 3, 4], 'y': [1, 4, 9, 16]}], 'layout': {'title': 'Plot generated in python'}}}

The dictionary seems to contain the data required to plot the figure in R. Could we display that kind of output as a plotly widget ?

title: should '$' and '[' behave differently for pandas DataFrames?
description:
E.g. in Python:

`````
```{python}
import pandas as pd
pdf = pd.DataFrame({"pop": [1]})
print(pdf["pop"]) # accesses pop column
print(pdf.pop)    # accesses pop DataFrame method
```
`````

However, for Python objects exposed to R, `[[` attempts to first access attributes rather than columns:

```
> library(reticulate)
> df <- data.frame(pop = 1)
> pdf <- r_to_py(df)
> pdf$pop
<bound method DataFrame.pop of    pop
0  1.0>
> pdf[["pop"]]
<bound method DataFrame.pop of    pop
0  1.0>
```

Should `[[` prefer accessing items rather than attributes for DataFrames?

I believe a similar question exists for Python dictionaries, and other objects implementing `__getitem__` in general.

title: Issue with translating DataFrame: py_ref_to_r(x) : Unsupported array conversion from 19
description:
Hi reticulate team,

First off, we love your product, and we know this issue will not be terribly easy to diagnose - apologies. We are trying to use reticulate with some pretty complex python bindings of some Java code we have. We've run into an issue getting things back into R that googling hasn't been able to solve. We won't be able to provide a minimal example that is easy to reproduce (unless you feel like installing our package, which has some nontrivial dependencies), but we will do our best to explain it here. 

We have a `Scenario` object with a method `par()` which returns in this case a `pandas.DataFrame` with three columns: 

```
In[11]:  scenario.par('interestrate')

Out[11]: 
  unit  value  year
0    %   0.05  2010
1    %   0.05  2020
2    %   0.05  2030
3    %   0.05  2040

In[12]: type(scenario.par('interestrate'))
Out[12]: pandas.core.frame.DataFrame

In[13]: scenario.par('interestrate').dtypes
Out[13]: 
unit      object
value    float32
year       int32
dtype: object
```

We get the following error using reticulate:

```
> scenario$par("interestrate")
Error in py_ref_to_r(x) : Unsupported array conversion from 19
```

It seems like we're hitting a [case/switch in `python.cpp`](https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/master/src/python.cpp#L844) where it's trying to translate unicode, but finding no specific case. 

Oddly enough, if we dump this object to csv and read it back in, all works:

foo.py:
```
import pandas as pd

def test_read():
    df =  pd.read_csv('~/test.csv')
    print(df)
    print(df.dtypes)
    return df
```

And this works:
```
import('foo')
foo$test_read()
```

Could you provide any guidance of how we might address this issue? We're happy to do type conversions etc on the Python side.

Cheers

title: `import_from_path` doesn't add to / remove from path properly
description:
`import_from_path` should:

* Guarantee to import from the specified path
* Not change the Python path globally

Currently, `import_from_path`:

* Only adds to the path if the specified path is not already there. Therefore, it does not control path ordering and cannot guarantee the library is imported from the specified path.
* Adds the path to the back of the path. Again, there are no guarantees - if another path contains the package, you'll get it from another path.
* does not remove the path before exiting the function

Suggested solution:

* Add to the front of the path, without checking
* Before exiting, remove from the front of the path.

title: Why is r/R not immediately initialized on the python side?
description:
I have a use case where I want to:

1) Create a function on the R side, `foo()`.
2) Create a function in a python script that calls `r.foo()`, call it `py_caller()`.
3) In R, use `source_python()` to source that script to gain access to `py_caller()`.
4) In R, call `py$py_caller()`.

I promise there is good reason for this.

The problem is that `r` is not initialized on the python side until a repl is started up. Once I run `repl_python()` and then `quit()` I can access the `r` object (I can tell this is the case because I can see it pop up in `py$r` after I run the repl), but before that I cannot and the code fails with `NameError: name 'r' is not defined`.

It seems that the `repl_python()` calls `eng_python_synchronize_before(globalenv())` which pushes R/r over to the python side. Is there any version of this you could add to `initialize_python()` so that we have immediate access to R from the python side without starting up a repl first?

title: `None` -> `NULL` conversion can break Pandas DF -> data.frame conversion
description:
When a Pandas Dataframe has a `None` value in one of the columns, the conversion to a data.frame fails. I think it has to do with the fact that you can't create a data frame out of a list of, in the case below, a vector and a `NULL`. The column isn't flattened all the way into a vector because of the `NULL`, and remains a list that can't be converted to a data.frame.

Please excuse the use of `pyarrow` to create the `None`. I'm not really sure how to do it otherwise from the reticulate side.

``` r
library(reticulate)
pd <- import("pandas", convert = FALSE)
pa <- import("pyarrow", convert = FALSE)

pa_array <- list(pa$array(list("hi", NULL)))
pa_tbl <- pa$Table$from_arrays(pa_array, list("col1"))
pd_df <- pa_tbl$to_pandas()

# Notice the None. This happens with stings and bools for sure
pd_df
#>    col1
#> 0    hi
#> 1  None

py_to_r(pd_df)
#> Error in (function (..., row.names = NULL, check.rows = FALSE, check.names = TRUE, : arguments imply differing number of rows: 1, 0


# Essentially what ends up happening is
hi_val <- pd_df$values$take(0)
none_val <- pd_df$values$take(1)

py_to_r(hi_val)
#> [1] "hi"
py_to_r(none_val)
#> NULL

as.data.frame(
  list(
    py_to_r(hi_val), 
    py_to_r(none_val)
  )
)
#> Error in (function (..., row.names = NULL, check.rows = FALSE, check.names = TRUE, : arguments imply differing number of rows: 1, 0
```

title: `delay_load` is effectively ignored  by `import_from_path()`
description:
A `delay_load = TRUE` argument to `import_from_path()` fails to have an effect.  `import_from_path()` imports the Python `sys` module to append the given `path`. This has the side effect of initializing Python:
https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/7c6bc9bd10ef4c040a6f311a6edd2942405dd085/R/python.R#L112-L118
So when the subsequent call to `import()` is made with `delay_load = TRUE`, the logic in `import()` sees that Python has been initialized and ignores `delay_load = TRUE`:

https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/7c6bc9bd10ef4c040a6f311a6edd2942405dd085/R/python.R#L55-L56

title: reticulate imports python2 before python3
description:
Hi,

I am developing a package `foo` which imports reticulate like this

```
#' Hello
#' @import reticulate
#' @export
myfunc = function() {
  import("mypackage")
  do stuff
}
```

When I use `devtools::load_all()` to test this package, I think reticulate is automatically being set up with python2, perhaps through detection of the roxygen @import reticulate. If I try to overwrite it using `use_python('/usr/local/bin/python3', required = TRUE)`, reticulate will still reference python2. However, if I start with a clean R session and source the function `myfunc` as a R script instead of as a package from devtools, I will be able to use python3. I suspect this is because sourcing it as an inline function does not trigger any kind of reticulate set up, and thus the python version doesn't get set yet.

The behavior I expected was

```
devtools::load_all()
use_python('/usr/local/bin/python3', required = TRUE)
myfunc() # will reference python 2, but should reference python3
```

title: pandas DataFrame with np.nan are not converted correctly
description:
Dear all,
I've stumbled with an issue with the way NA are encoded in Python: it seems that the clasical way is to use np.nan whatever the data type as described in https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/missing_data.html. This is the convention used by pd.read_csv for instance. When the data type is a "string" this leads to an issue: reticulate fails to convert such a DataFrame as shown in the following example
```
library(reticulate)

py_run_string('import pandas as pd')
py_run_string('import numpy as np')
py_run_string('date = ["2017/01/12", np.nan]')
py_run_string('data = {"date" : date}')
py_run_string('df = pd.DataFrame(data)')
py_run_string('dfcol = df["date"]')

py$df
py$dfcol
```
It seems that the column is converted as a list and not to a vector with missing data which seems to be the expected behavior from a Python user perspective.

Yours;

Erwan

> By default, the version of Python found on the system PATH is checked first, and then some other conventional location for Py Python (e.g. /usr/local/bin/python, /opt/local/bin/python, etc.) are checked.

For debugging purposes, it would be useful to have a command like `which_python` which returns the current `python` being used

title: What should `NA` be converted to in Python?
description:
Currently `NA` is converted to Python as `True` which doesn't make too much sense. This is because `NA` is logical in R.
```
> class(NA)
[1] "logical"
> r_to_py(NA)
True
```

Perhaps we should treat it as `np.nan` (similar to R's `NaN`) since that's the representation Python users use for missing data, e.g. [missing data in pandas objects](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/missing_data.html)? 
```
> r_to_py(NaN)
nan
```

"`NaN` is the the default missing value marker for reasons of computational speed and convenience. However, if you want to consider `inf` and `-inf` to be "NA" in computations, you can set `pandas.options.mode.use_inf_as_na = True`" ([source](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/missing_data.html#values-considered-missing)). So this might be something we need to keep in mind when deciding how we approach this.

title: Minor Clarification in Calling Python from R article
description:
The [Calling Python from R](https://rstudio.github.io/reticulate/articles/calling_python.html) has the following snippets

```
main <- import_main()

py <- import_builtins()
py$print('foo')

```
Further down there is the snippet
```
library(reticulate)

py_run_file("script.py")

py_run_string("x = 10")

# access the python main module via the 'py' object
py$x
```
It might be worth mentioning that this snippet works only when the previous snippet is not run. If the previous snippet is run were `py` is assigned from `import_builtins()`, the syntax to use is `main$x` instead of `py$x`

Also in arrays section, the following snippet gives an error
```
a <- np_array(c(1:8), dim = c(2,4), order = "C")
```

title: Memory leak in assigning R variables to Python space
description:
When assigning values from R to Python's __main__ with

`py$x <- rVar`

each iterative assignment consumes more memory until the system runs out of memory and it crashes.  To reproduce:

```
library(reticulate)
main <- import_main(convert = FALSE)

for(i in 1:10){
  main$x <- rep(0,5000000)
  py_run_string("
del x
import gc
gc.collect()")
}
```
Each iteration of this loop increases memory use of rsession by ~200MB which is never released.  In comparison, if we generate the variable inside Python it does not cause the same issue:

```
library(reticulate)
py_run_string("")

for(i in 1:10){
  py_run_string(
  "
x=[0]*5000000
del x
import gc
gc.collect()")
}
```

Similarly, calling a Python function on a large R variable does not cause the issue either.  As a result, the following workaround prevents memory leaks:

```
py_run_string(
'
def load_global(x,n):
    globals()[n]=x
'
)
py$load_global(rep(0,5000000),'x')
```

title: Include option bug
description:
Hello I found a possible bug in reticulate library.

**Problem**
Testing this code:
***************************************
\documentclass{article}
\begin{document}
<<R_test,include=FALSE,split=T,fig.path="./", eval=T,echo=T>>=
a=10
print(a)
@
Including the external results from file R\_text.tex produces:

a=10
print(a)
@
Including the external results from file Py\_text.tex produces:

\input{./Py_test}
\end{document}
*****************************************

Running this Rnw file produces:
**Including the external results from file R text.tex produces**
**a=10**
**print(a)**
**## [1] 10**

**Including the external results from file Py text.tex produces:**
**a=10**
**print(a)**

**Description**
In this code I need that the **results and source code**  from python and R goes to an external files.  

Those files must be included in some latex file later using the **include** key.

The R chunk write to R tex file the source code and the output (**##[1] 10**).
But the Python chunk only produces the source code, never the output from any print.

Running in R it works great.
Running the Python do not.

**Solution.**
I downloaded your reticulate library from github:

 **git clone https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate.git**

and I change this:

FILE: knitr-engine.R
Before:
Lines 144 and 145:
     **# append captured outputs
      if (nzchar(captured) && isTRUE(options$include))**

After:
Lines 144 and 145:
   **# append captured outputs
      if (nzchar(captured) && isTRUE(options$eval))**

Then I did
 **R CMD build reticulate**
and
**R CMD INSTALL ./reticulate_1.5.0.9004.tar.gz**

Now it work OK.
The output now using the same code is:
**Including the external results from file R text.tex produces:**
**a=10**
**print(a)**
**## [1] 10**
**Including the external results from file Py text.tex produces:**
**a=10**
**print(a)**
**## 10**

Now the **##10** is present.
I write many documents using R with Sweave to produce PDF, and this options are very common to put the results in specifics point in the TEX files. 

According to the knit documentation i**nclude=FALSE** and **split=TRUE**, produces the output to a file but not include it in LATEX final code.

The options **eval=TRUE**, produces the output (of print cat, etc) and **echo=TRUE** produces the source code.

According to this **include=FALSE** must not disable the output results. This is the way that R works.

I do not have access to your GIT HUB to make the change and I need to verify this situation.

Please let me know if this information is correct.

Thanks
Freddy Rojas.
Costa Rica

title: reconcile differences in indexes between R, Python
description:
There is some tension between 0-based and 1-based indexing here...

Compare e.g.

```R
> df <- data.frame(x = c("a", "b", "c"), y = c("d", "e", "f"))
> pdf <- r_to_py(df)

> df
  x y
1 a d
2 b e
3 c f

> pdf
   x  y
0  a  d
1  b  e
2  c  f
```

Note that the Python index goes from 0:2. In fact, under the hood it's really just a 'range' that can provide values in that range:

```
> pdf$index
RangeIndex(start=0, stop=3, step=1)
```

But then consider the following behavior:

```r
pdf <- pd$DataFrame(list(x = pd$Series(1:3, index = 10:12)))
```

```r
> pdf
    x
10  1
11  2
12  3

> py_to_r(pdf)
   x
10 1
11 2
12 3
```

It might be surprising at first glance that in one case the index is changing, while in the other case it is not. Any thoughts on how we should reconcile this?

title: arithmetic operators for Python objects
description:
[Link to SO post](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/49056372/arcpy-map-algebra-from-reticulate)

I came across this issue trying to use the ArcGIS module `arcpy`, but I suspect there are a few other places where this could be an issue. Basically, arithmetic operators for Python objects don't work for their R counterparts unless they can be type converted. 

I was thinking one solution would be to use the S3 system to add methods to the arithmetic operators for the `python.builtin.object` class, which would call the corresponding arithmetic operator function from the `operator` module:

```
`+.default` = .Primitive('+')
`+.python.builtin.object` = function(e1, e2) {
  op = import("operator")
  op$add(e1, e2)
}
`+` = function (e1, e2) UseMethod('+')
```

But converting the R operators to S3 methods seems... drastic. A more moderated approach would be to define a set of Python operators e.g. `%py+%`, `%py-%`, etc. that would use the Python operators instead of the R primitives.

```
`%py+%` = function(e1, e2) {
  op = import("operator")
  op$add(e1, e2)
}
```

But I don't know how we could enforce order of operations with this strategy.

Should py_to_r() copy over attributes?
description:
I'm playing around with the `pendulum` python library, and wanted to write a wrapper for a `pendulum` `Date` that transformed it into an R `Date`.

I discovered `py_to_r()` and the underlying S3, `py_to_r_wrapper` and tried something like:

``` r
library(reticulate)
library(magrittr)
pend <- import("pendulum")

d1 <- pend$Date(2013L, 01L, 01L)

class(d1)
#> [1] "pendulum.date.Date"                       
#> [2] "pendulum.mixins.default.TranslatableMixin"

#> [4] "pendulum.mixins.default.TestableMixin"

  x$year
}

  x$month
}
pend_day <- function(x) {
  x$day
}

# Wrapper for conversion
py_to_r_wrapper.pendulum.date.Date <- function(x) {

py_to_r_2(d1)

I assume this is not intended? Or am I just doing something wrong?

title: R on Windows segfaults on dyn.unload of reticulate.dll
description:
If I load reticulate in R on Windows, do some python operations
(initializing python), and then explicitly dyn.unload reticulate.dll,
then R crashes with a segfault, as in the following (using R 3.4.3,
reticulate 1.4):

    > library(reticulate)
    > import("sys")$version
    [1] "3.6.3 |Anaconda, Inc.| (default, Oct 15 2017, 03:27:45) [MSC v.1900 64 bit (AMD64)]"
    > dyn.unload(getLoadedDLLs()$reticulate[["path"]])
    > Segmentation fault

I suspect that the segfault occurs because unloading the DLL doesn't
shut down some python thread that eventually tries to access the DLL
memory.  Notice that the segfault above occurs after the console
prompt is printed, some time after dyn.unload is executed.

I discovered this problem when using reticulate in the TERR
R-compatible engine, which would sometimes give an error when quitting
the console.  I believe this happens because TERR currently unloads
any loaded DLLs before exiting.  I suspect that this doesn't happen
when exiting R because R just shuts down the engine with 'exit'
without unloading DLLs first.

I propose that reticulate.dll include clean-up code to shut down
python when it is unloaded.

title: Incorrect Conversion of R Function Signature
description:
Many Python packages check the signature of the function that's being passed in as a parameter. However, reticulate doesn't convert the signature correctly. 

A couple of issues:

- Currently even though an R function does not have any keywords arguments, after it's converted to Python function, it will have keyword args. Some relevant code [here](https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/ff9373383a07c313fc7dae98d19ff17e8b6cdae4/src/python.cpp#L1292) and [here](https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/ff9373383a07c313fc7dae98d19ff17e8b6cdae4/inst/python/rpytools/call.py#L13). 
- The names of the function arguments are not reserved. Recall that we had to do [this](https://github.com/rstudio/tfestimators/blob/master/inst/python/estimatortools/functions.py) in tfestimators to make sure the signature is correct.

title: clarify that Python must be compiled with shared library support
description: @jjallaire's comment [here](https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/issues/98#issuecomment-334960171) states that **`reticulate`** needs to bind to the Python shared library, which implies that the shared library needs to exist. If Python is compiled from source without the `--enable-shared` flag, this will not be the case. I was not able to find this shared library requirement explicitly mentioned in the **`reticulate`** documentation, so it might be helpful to add it, possibly in the [Python Version Configuration](https://rstudio.github.io/reticulate/articles/versions.html) vignette.

Assign

Possible actions:
1: abort (with core dump, if enabled)
2: normal R exit
3: exit R without saving workspace
4: exit R saving workspace
```

It looks like the attempt to unload the `reticulate` namespace, as per `devtools:::unload("reticulate")`, causes the crash. I imagine it's because the Python session itself has loaded some separate modules, and those also need to be unloaded before `reticulate` itself can be unloaded.

This is sort of an edge case (it will only affect users who are developing `reticulate` using this workflow, or others who try to reload the `reticulate` namespace for some reason) so I don't think it will be that common in practice, but felt it was worth documenting the issue for posterity in case we want to fix it down the line.

title: provide mechanism for submitting incomplete lines to Python console
description:
Motivation: I'm trying to write a `knitr` engine for `reticulate` that allows for the interleaving of code input and outputs. To that end, I think it's necessary to be able to submit code line-by-line to the Python session -- for example:


    ```{python}
    x = 1
    print(x)

    y = 2
    print(y)
    ```

It would be great if we were able to run code line-by-line here, capturing outputs as lines are executed, so that the output of each `print` statement is shown immediately below the associated statement. (This would hopefully include generated images down the line as well; not just console output)

One thing that makes this a bit trickier is multi-line statements, e.g.

```{python}
x = [[1, 2, 3],
     [4, 5, 6],
     [7, 8, 9]]
```

Is there any way for us to submit a line to the Python console, and get a console 'status' back (e.g. incomplete input vs. complete input and so on)? It seems like this isn't provided by `py_run_string()` so I'm wondering if there's a somewhat lower-level / more nuanced API we can use here.

title: the non-standard evaluation done by 'dict()' leads to unexpected behavior
description:
Small example I bumped into while using `tfestimators`:

```R
library(reticulate)
library(tfestimators)

age <- column_numeric("age")
height <- column_numeric("height")

train_data <- data.frame(
  age = c(29, 38, 42),
  height = c(180, 190, 170)
)

dict(train_data)
```

This gives:

```R
> dict(train_data)
{_NumericColumn(key='height', shape=(1,), default_value=None, dtype=tf.float32, normalizer_fn=None): [180.0, 190.0, 170.0], _NumericColumn(key='age', shape=(1,), default_value=None, dtype=tf.float32, normalizer_fn=None): [29.0, 38.0, 42.0]}
```

when I expected the keys would remain as-is as named strings.

This seems like a relatively dangerous landmine. I recall this behavior was implemented as arbitrary Python objects can be keys within a Python dictionary, but I wonder if we should instead consider a more explicit mechanism for requesting this behavior?

title: Document the difference in handing character data in Python 2 vs 3.
description:
Python 2 wrongly assumes all character data is `latin-1` encoded, so when you call Python methods returning character data from reticulate w/ Py 2.x, you get a R character vector.
But in Python 3 finally the py devs figured it out that not the whole world speaks English and uses `latin-1` char. set ;).
So if you call a Python method returning character data from reticulate w/ Py 3.x you may get a wrapped object for the `bytes` class, which you need to explicitly decode using the proper char. encoding. The onus is on the calling function to know what the encoding is and not have Python erroneously assume the encoding. This is especially true when the python function is calling external APIs, database calls etc. 

This needs to be documented for reticulate users who may be using the package under Py 2.x / 3.x, so that they understand the difference http://python-notes.curiousefficiency.org/en/latest/python3/text_file_processing.html.

title: Having python 2.6 causes the package to not load
description:

The image that appveyor uses to build R packages (via r-appveyor) has many python versions installed.
https://www.appveyor.com/docs/build-environment/#python. From 2.6 to latest 3.5

The trouble is reticulate is not compatible with 2.6 (2.6 doesn't have `sysconfig` module which came only in 2.7). Now the default path has python 2.7, but for some reason unknown to me , when doing `library(reticulate)`, python 2.6 is used for the initial stuff. I think is is even before `py_discover()` or `use_python()` comes in to play.  And so the package can't be loaded.

You can see https://github.com/krlmlr/r-appveyor/issues/91 for full error details. I am not even sure if having RETICULATE_PYTHON=<python 2.7+> will help in this case, as the path already have python 2.7 in it.

I think one thing reticulate can do is skip python < 2.7 as part of it's initial load even if it finds it.

title: How to deal with infinite iterators / generators ?
description:
Some Python functions return infinite iterators / generators ( `keras::flow_images_from_data()`, for example).
For such iterators / generators, `reticulate::iterate()` gets into an infinite loop, and it cannot be used in R's `for` loops as in native Python's `for` loops.

An obvious solution to the problem is to use Python's built-in `next()` function, but it seems a bit awkward because `next` is a keyword in R and you must quote it to call from R.

Do you have any better idea for the problem ?

```r
library(reticulate)

py <- import_builtins()

# create an infinite generator
main <- py_run_string("
def foo():
    n = 0
    while True:
        yield n
        n += 1
")
it <- main$foo()

# This gets into an infinite loop
for(i in iterate(it)) {
  print(i)
  if(i >= 10) break
}

# It works, but seems a bit awkward
while(TRUE) {
  i <- py$`next`(it)
  print(i)
  if(i >= 10) break
}

```

title: Error: R is already initialized
description:
This is a minor issue I ran into when executing an R script that uses reticulate, in a project that uses `rpy2` to interface with R from python elsewhere.

Posting here in case others come across the same issue.

I have a test function in R called `validate_setup`:

```r
library(reticulate)
validate_setup <- function(verbose = TRUE, test_packages = c('numpy', 'cohorts')) {
  # report on py_config
  if (verbose)
     print(reticulate::py_config())

  # check availability of package(s)
  for (pkg in test_packages) {
    if (verbose)
       print(paste0('checking that ', pkg, ' is available'))
    if (!reticulate::py_available(pkg))
       stop(paste0('python package could not be found: ', pkg))
  }

  # check python initialized
  if (verbose)
     print('checking that python is initialized')
  reticulate::py_config()
  reticulate:::ensure_python_initialized()

  # load package
  for (pkg in test_packages) {
    if (verbose)
      print(paste0('loading ', pkg))
    dummy <- reticulate::import(pkg, convert = FALSE)
  }
  print("setup OK")
}
```

I also have a trivial command-line wrapper script to execute this called `run_validate_setup.R`

I can execute this using in one of two python environments:

1. **testenv1**: includes only cohorts: 

    ```sh
     conda create -n testenv1 python=3 scipy numpy pandas

     pip install cohorts
     Rscript run_validate_setup.R
     ```

2. **testenv2**: includes cohorts & rpy2:

    ```sh

In the first virtualenv, I have no problems:

#' subdirectory thereof. If `model_dir` is not set, a temporary directory is
#' used. The `config` argument can be passed `RunConfig` object containing information
#' about the execution environment. It is passed on to the `model_fn`, if the
#' `model_fn` has a parameter named "config" (and input functions in the same
#' manner). If the `config` parameter is not passed, it is instantiated by the
#' `Estimator`. Not passing config means that defaults useful for local execution
#' are used. `Estimator` makes config available to the model (for instance, to

Follows the signature:     * Args:       * `features`: single `Tensor` or `dict` of `Tensor`s              (depending on data passed to `train`),       * `labels`: `Tensor` or `dict` of `Tensor`s (for multi-head              models). If mode is `ModeKeys.PREDICT`, `labels=NULL` will be              passed. If the `model_fn`'s signature does not accept              `mode`, the `model_fn` must still be able to handle              `labels=NULL`.       * `mode`: Optional. Specifies if this training, evaluation or              prediction. See `ModeKeys`.       * `params`: Optional `dict` of hyperparameters.  Will receive what              is passed to Estimator in `params` parameter. This allows              to configure Estimators from hyper parameter tuning.       * `config`: Optional configuration object. Will receive what is passed              to Estimator in `config` parameter, or the default `config`.              Allows updating things in your model_fn based on configuration              such as `num_ps_replicas`, or `model_dir`.

If `NULL`, the model_dir in     `config` will be used if set. If both are set, they must be same. If     both are `NULL`, a temporary directory will be used.

title: [Off-Topic] Use sympy to provide symbolic computation in R
description:
Firstly I want to really thank Allaire and RStudio people for all their significant works, including this remarkable package. It is also good to know that reticulate is already on CRAN.

An idea in my mind is to bring symbolic computation capacity to R, possibly by wrapping the [sympy](http://www.sympy.org/en/index.html) python library. We know that R is not designed for symbolic computation, however it does not limit the attempt to bring such capacity. One example that I previously looking at is the [SymPy](https://github.com/JuliaPy/SymPy.jl) package for julia, but I think it is possible to provide a more seamlessly integration of sympy to R, with reticulate. And I think it is even possible that the R's wrapper can be more convenient than the python package itself -- due to the lazy evaluation nature of R, we may use some syntax magic to define a symbolic expression without declaring variables, etc..

In fact, reticulate already provides seamlessly interface to python functions, we can further substitute R's binary operators and math functions using group generics in order to work with sympy variables. We may also provide ways to convert a symbolic expression to a R function (as the julia package SymPy does) and other convenient functions to work with symbolic computation.

I have done some experiment with the idea (see https://github.com/Marlin-Na/symbolicR), due to the limited time and also my limited experience, I have not managed to provide a relative complete prototype so far.


But my question is:

How do you think about the idea that bring sympy to R with reticulate? Or did you have such plan when you created the reticulate package?

Thanks!

title: append all Python class bases to R class attribute
description:
When executing a python function with reticulate, class information from the python object is appended to the resulting R object's class attribute. This is done in the CPP function [`py_ref`](https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/master/src/python.cpp#L229).

If I understand this code correctly, `py_ref` [grabs the `__class__`](https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/master/src/python.cpp#L247-L248) attribute of the python object (the class of which this is an *instance*), as well as [the parent class](https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/master/src/python.cpp#L252-L257) from which this class inherits, via the class object's `.__bases__` attribute. **However this is only done for the immediate parent class, not for the full inheritance.**

---

I am working on a port of the [`GPflow`](https://github.com/GPflow/GPflow) Python module, and want to map its nice kernel creation syntax to R. Kernel objects can be added, multiplied etc., and the `GPflow` module enables this by defining addition for all objects of class `Kern`. for example, in python:

```python
import GPflow as gp
k1 = gp.kernels.Constant(1)
k2 = gp.kernels.Bias(1)
k3 = gp.kernels.Cosine(1)
K = k1 + k2 + k3
```
The full class inheritance for these objects is:
`k1`: `object`>`Parentable`>`Parameterized`>`Kern`>`Static`>`Constant`
`k2`: `object`>`Parentable`>`Parameterized`>`Kern`>`Static`>`Constant`>`Bias`
`k3`: `object`>`Parentable`>`Parameterized`>`Kern`>`Stationary`>`Cosine`
The `+` operator is a wrapper around `GPflow.kernels.Add((k1, k2, k3))`, defined in the `Kern` class; it works for any class instance inheriting from `Kern`.

To enable the same syntax in an R port using reticulate, it would be really helpful for `GPflow.kernels.Kern` to be listed in the class attribute for the corresponding R objects, so we can do S3 dispatch. But because only the immediate parent class is returned this isn't currently possible. I.e. in R:

```r
library(reticulate)
gp <- import('GPflow')
k1 <- gp$kernels$Constant(1)
k2 <- gp$kernels$Bias(1)
k3 <- gp$kernels$Cosine(1)
class(k1); class(k2); class(k3)
```
```
[1] "GPflow.kernels.Constant" "GPflow.kernels.Static"   "python.builtin.object"  
[1] "GPflow.kernels.Bias"     "GPflow.kernels.Constant" "python.builtin.object"
[1] "GPflow.kernels.Cosine"     "GPflow.kernels.Stationary" "python.builtin.object" 
```

---

A fix would be to have [this section of `py_ref`](https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/master/src/python.cpp#L252-L257) recurse through the parent classes, finding their parents (via the `.__bases__` attribute) and adding them to the R object's class attribute, until hitting either `object` or an empty string (`object`'s parent class).

As far as I can tell, there is no sane way of doing this from the reticulate-wrapping GPflow-specific R package.

If that sounds like behaviour you would like (or tolerate) in `reticulate`, I'd be happy to do a PR (though my C++ is decidedly rusty so very happy if someone else wants to do it!).

title: Numpy Arrays and R Arrays are printed differently
description:
Say you have a (4,2) array in R, and you convert to Python then print. This works as expected.

```r
> R_4_2 <- array(1:prod(4,2), dim = c(4,2))
#     [,1] [,2]
#[1,]    1    5
#[2,]    2    6
#[3,]    3    7
#[4,]    4    8
> dim(R_4_2)
#[1] 4 2
> Np_4_2 <- np$array(R_4_2)
> Np_4_2
#[[1 5]
# [2 6]
# [3 7]
# [4 8]]
> Np_4_2$shape
#(4, 2)
```
Now say we'd like to extend our original R array so instead of being a single (4,2) matrix we want it to be a 3 (4,2) matrices. In R we tack on the extra dimension to the end of the shape array.

```r
> R_4_2_3 <- array(1:prod(4,2,3), dim = c(4,2,3))
#, , 1
#
#     [,1] [,2]
#[1,]    1    5
#[2,]    2    6
#[3,]    3    7
#[4,]    4    8
#
#, , 2
#
#     [,1] [,2]
#[1,]    9   13
#[2,]   10   14
#[3,]   11   15
#[4,]   12   16
#
#, , 3
#
#     [,1] [,2]
#[1,]   17   21
#[2,]   18   22
#[3,]   19   23
#[4,]   20   24
> dim(R_4_2_3)
#[1] 4 2 3
```
This time when we convert to Numpy the shape is the same, but instead of printing 3 (4,2) matrices, we print 4 (3,2) matrices

```r
> Np_4_2_3 <- np$array(R_4_2_3)
> Np_4_2_3$shape
#(4, 2, 3)
> Np_4_2_3
#[[[ 1  9 17]
#  [ 5 13 21]]
#
# [[ 2 10 18]
#  [ 6 14 22]]
#
# [[ 3 11 19]
#  [ 7 15 23]]
#
# [[ 4 12 20]
#  [ 8 16 24]]]
```
The equivalent shape in numpy that would print out the same way as R would be a (3,4,2). I'm not sure what the best way to solve this. Could we change the default behavior of arrays in R?

title: Inconsistency between tf.matmul in Python and tf$matmul in R
description:
_From @G-Lynn on February 13, 2017 23:31_

Attached is a simple example of an issue in using matmul to multiply an array of matrices in R.  I think the issue is a discrepancy in the way that the shape argument works in the R and python version.  

I am trying to use the tf$matmul function to multiply an array of matrices by an array of vectors.  As an example, I am trying to multiply [1, 2; 3, 4] * [1; 2] and [5,6; 7,8] * [3; 4].  The example works as expected in Python, but in the TensorFlow API for R, a dimension error is generated.  

In Python, the code for the example is:
############# Beginning of Python code
import tensorflow as tf
a = tf.constant(np.arange(1, 9, dtype=np.int32),shape=[2, 2, 2])  #create array of 2 matrices each 2x2: (1,2; 3,4) and (5,6; 7,8)
b = tf.constant(np.arange(1, 5, dtype=np.int32),shape=[2, 2, 1]) #multuply each of the matrices by a 2x1 vector (1,2)' and (3,4)' 
sess = tf.Session()
sess.run(a)
c = tf.matmul(a, b)
sess.run(a)
sess.run(b)
sess.run(c)  #the answer is the correct set of 2x1 vectors (5,11)' and (39,53)'
############# End of Python Code

When I try to implement this same example in R, an error is produced due to a difference in the way the dimensions of the arrays are indexed in the shape argument.  

##################### Begin R Code
rm(list = ls())
devtools::install_github("rstudio/tensorflow")
library(tensorflow)

#Create an array of 3 matrices
A = list(matrix(1:4, nrow=2, byrow=T), matrix(5:8, nrow=2, byrow=T))
A = array(unlist(A), dim=c(2,2,2) )  #2 matrices of dimension 2x2
B = array(1:4, dim = c(2,1,2) )  #2 vectors of 2x1
A_tf = tf$constant(A, dtype="float64", shape=c(2,2,2))  
B_tf = tf$constant(B, dtype="float64", shape=c(2,1,2))
sess = tf$Session()
sess$run(A_tf)
sess$run(B_tf)
sess$run(tf$matmul(A_tf,B_tf))

################## End R code

I believe the error is because of a discrepancy in the way that the shape argument works in tf$constant (R) and the way the shape argument works in tf.constant (R).  In R, the number of elements in the array is the last argument in shape so that  shape = c(2,1,3) means an array with 3 2x1 vectors.  In the python implementation, the number of array elements is the first argument so that shape=[3, 2, 1]  means 3 vectors of 2x1.  

When the function tf$matmul(A_tf,B_tf) is called, I think the difference in indexing the shapes of the array is causing an error. 

Thanks for your attention.   






_Copied from original issue: rstudio/tensorflow#88_

title: Python object instantiation fails for classes defined in an R session
description:

I tried to create a new class with Python's builtin `type()` function, but the class caused segfault when it was instantiated.

```r
library(reticulate)
py <- import("__builtin__")
Foo1 <- py$type("Foo1", tuple(), dict(a=1, f=function(self, x) x+1))
Foo1

```r
main <- py_run_string("
Foo2 = type('Foo2', (), {'a': 1, 'f': lambda self, x: x+1})
")
Foo2 <- environment(main$Foo2)$attrib
Foo2
#> <class '__main__.Foo2'>
foo2 <- py_call(Foo2, list())
foo2$a
